pool.q: A patient has a white cataract. In addition to the standard supplies and instruments for cataract surgery, what should the surgeon have ready for use in this patient?
pool.rationale: The surgeon should always be prepared for likely complications by having alternative surgical plans ready and the appropriate instruments available in the operating room. Staining the capsule of a white cataract aids in direct visualization and promotes creation of a controlled continuous curvilinear capsulorrhexis (CCC). Trypan blue dye would certainly be advantageous for capsular staining. If a pupil is miotic or there is zonular weakness, the surgeon should be ready to use other devices as the situation dictates.

pool.q: What postoperative complication may result from the creation of a 7.0 mm capsulorrhexis during cataract surgery?
pool.rationale: The creation of an overly large (7.0 mm)  capsulorrhexis is a well-known risk factor for IOL dislocation. Other factors include haptic damage, zonular defects, or placement of a 1-piece IOL in the sulcus. Capsular block syndrome occurs when OVD remains posterior to the IOL, causing an anterior shift of the IOL and myopic shift, but it is not associated with a large capsulorrhexis. IOL glistenings have been implicated in piggybacking lenses, in which a large capsulorrhexis may reduce the incidence. Capsular phimosis occurs with a small capsulorrhexis, not a large one.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Lens & Cataract — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: The risk of what intraoperative occurrence is increased during phacoemulsification of the type of cataract demonstrated in the figure?
pool.rationale:
A weak or absent area of posterior capsule in a posterior polar cataract increases the risk of capsular rupture during cataract surgery. For this reason, avoiding complete hydrodissection in order to avoid excessive pressure build-up and possible tearing of the capsule beneath the opacity may be advisable. Gentle hydrodelineation using small volumes of fluid may be preferable. It is also recommended to remove epinuclear and/or cortical material in the vicinity of the posterior polar opacity last in the event of absent posterior capsule in this area. In some situations, it may be safer to leave a firmly adherent posterior polar opacity and treat this area postoperatively with a Nd:YAG capsulotomy.
There is no associated increased risk of iris prolapse, poor pupillary dilation, or capsulorrhexis extension among patients with posterior polar cataracts.

pool.q: During cataract surgery there is a large break in the posterior capsule. The decision is made to place an intraocular lens (IOL) in the ciliary sulcus. Why should a 3-piece IOL be used instead of a single-piece acrylic IOL?

options.a: The larger haptics on the single-piece acrylic IOL can make contact with and weaken the zonular fibers, causing a dislocation of the IOL in the future.
options.b: Placing a single-piece acrylic IOL in the sulcus will lead to excess myopic shift due to the planar nature of that IOL, as opposed to the posterior vaulting of a 3-piece IOL.
options.c: The larger haptics on the single-piece acrylic IOL can make contact with uveal tissues and lead to uveitis-glaucoma-hyphema (UGH) syndrome.
options.d: The planar nature of the single-piece acrylic lens makes it difficult to perform optic capture within the capsulorhexis when the IOL is placed in the ciliary sulcus.

pool.rationale:
A single-piece acrylic IOL has large haptics that can make contact with uveal tissues, causing uveitis-glaucoma-hyphema (UGH) syndrome. Damage to the zonules and late dislocation due to the haptics has not been reported.
Single-piece acrylic IOLs  are planar and not posteriorly vaulted like 3-piece IOLs. However, any IOL placed in the sulcus without optic capture will have more effective refracting power. Therefore, the power of the IOL should be decreased. If one is planning to capture the optic in the capsulorhexis, the IOL power should not be changed.
Single-piece acrylic IOLs are very flexible, and optic capture could easily be performed. Because of the issue of the haptics in the sulcus, however, it is not advisable to do so. Some surgeons have described a "reverse optic capture," where the single-piece acrylic haptics are placed into the capsular bag and the optic is brought forward through the capsulorhexis. This is useful if the capsule is broken, but the surgeon still wants to use the single-piece acrylic IOL, such as when a multifocal IOL was planned. It has also been described as a technique to reduce negative dysphotopsia after cataract surgery.

pool.q: What is the mechanism for hypotony following a traumatic cyclodialysis cleft?
pool.rationale: Cyclodialysis is the separation of the ciliary body from its insertion at the scleral spur. It can occur as a result of trauma or of surgical manipulation of intraocular tissue. Repair of a cyclodialysis cleft is often indicated to relieve prolonged hypotony. Hypotony is caused by the increased uveoscleral outflow because it is anatomically a separation at its insertion, not an increase in trabecular outflow. Aqueous misdirection is a cause of elevated intraocular pressure (IOP), not hypotony. Uveitis can sometimes cause increased IOP and sometimes decreased IOP, but generally not enough to cause hypotony.

pool.q: What systemic disorder increases the likelihood of developing a posterior subcapsular cataract?
pool.rationale: Diabetes mellitus is associated with accelerated development of all age-related lens changes, including posterior subcapsular cataract. The proposed pathophysiologic reasons for these changes are multifactorial, including increased lens hydration from sorbitol accumulation, glycation of lens proteins, and increased oxidative stress. Systemic hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, and ischemic cardiovascular disease are not associated with increased risk for developing posterior subcapsular cataract, although these conditions may be relevant for evaluation of general health and for preoperative planning for cataract surgery.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Lens & Cataract — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: In a patient with postoperative corneal edema, what finding would suggest that a toxin introduced intraoperatively caused the edema?
pool.rationale: Toxic anterior segment syndrome (TASS) is generally characterized by diffuse limbus-to-limbus corneal edema. Pain that is typically less than the pain experienced with endophthalmitis is also a feature of TASS. Marked decrease in vision and wrinkles in Descemet membrane are nonspecific for TASS.

pool.q: What method would be useful in distinguishing the effect of corneal disease on visual acuity in a patient with both anterior basement membrane dystrophy and cataract?
pool.rationale:
The thickened epithelium and redundant basement membrane of anterior basement membrane dystrophy, when present in the visual axis, results in irregular corneal astigmatism. A trial of gas-permeable contact lens can mask this irregular astigmatism and help determine its effect on visual impairment.
Potential acuity estimation does not distinguish between corneal and lenticular causes for blurred vision.
Computerized corneal topography and anterior segment optical coherence tomography help in the diagnosis of anterior basement dystrophy.

pool.q: A patient with visually significant cataract and the corneal problem depicted in the figure presents to the ophthalmologist's office. What surgical plan and technique should be considered for this patient?

options.a: Femtosecond laser-assisted cataract surgery with astigmatic keratotomy
options.b: Removal of the corneal lesion, with subsequent cataract surgery 3 months later
options.c: Performing cataract surgery, with toric intraocular lens (IOL) placement

pool.rationale: The pterygium depicted in the image would cause a significant impact on the patient's vision and on the ophthalmologist's ability to obtain accurate keratometry for cataract surgery. The best approach would be to remove the pterygium and wait at least 6 weeks for the keratometry to stabilize before proceeding with cataract surgery. Ultrasound biometry would not lead to more accurate lens calculations in this setting.

pool.q: On the first day following uncomplicated phacoemulsification, an increase in intraocular pressure (IOP) is noted. What is the most likely etiology?
pool.rationale:
A mild, self-limited rise in IOP is common following cataract surgery. However, a significant and sustained elevation may require timely management. Ophthalmic viscosurgical devices (OVDs) retained in the eye after cataract surgery are frequently responsible for early postoperative IOP elevation, which peaks 4 to 6 hours after surgery. The large molecules of the viscoelastic material can impair aqueous outflow through the trabecular meshwork. Even when all apparent OVD is removed from the anterior chamber, residual OVD, particularly dispersive agents, can lodge in the posterior chamber or behind the lens implant. All types of OVDs, but in particular the higher-viscosity agents, may cause the pressure to rise. IOP elevation usually does not last more than a few days and is amenable to medical treatment. The clinician may quickly manage marked IOP elevation in the early postoperative period by applying gentle pressure on the posterior lip of a preexisting paracentesis incision to release a small amount of aqueous humor. Topical and/or systemic pressure-lowering agents should also be administered, as IOP reduction after aqueous release is short-lived, with the IOP likely to rise again within 1 to 2 hours of the decompression.
Elevated IOP without angle closure after cataract surgery may be caused by hyphema, toxic anterior segment syndrome (TASS), endophthalmitis, retained lens material (phacolytic or phacoantigenic [formerly termed phacoanaphylactic] reactions), uveitis, iris pigment release, preexisting glaucoma, corticosteroid use, vitreous in the anterior chamber, ghost cell glaucoma, or a-chymotrypsin use. Angle-closure glaucoma may be due to pupillary block, ciliary block, epithelial ingrowth, neovascular glaucoma, or peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS). Treating the underlying cause of the IOP elevation should be curative.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Lens & Cataract — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: How does toxic anterior segment syndrome (TASS) differ in presentation from other causes of postoperative inflammation?

options.a: TASS is more likely to present at postoperative day one.
options.b: Patients with TASS are more likely to have a hypopyon.
options.c: Pain is likely to be more severe in patients with TASS
options.d: Corneal edema in TASS is generally limited to the central cornea.

pool.rationale: The symptoms and signs of TASS may mimic those of infectious endophthalmitis and include photophobia, severe reduction in visual acuity, corneal edema, and marked anterior chamber reaction, occasionally with hypopyon. TASS presents within hours of surgery, whereas acute infectious endophthalmitis typically develops 2 to 7 days postoperatively. Other potentially distinguishing features of TASS include diffuse, limbus-to-limbus corneal edema; anterior chamber fibrinous exudate; a dilated, irregular, or nonreactive pupil; and elevated IOP. The pathologic changes are limited to the anterior chamber. Pain is typically much milder than that experienced with an infection. If endophthalmitis is suspected, diagnostic and therapeutic interventions should be undertaken.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Lens & Cataract — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient with a history of radial keratotomy (RK) undergoes cataract surgery. What potential issue should the surgeon anticipate?
pool.rationale: RK incisions typically swell after cataract surgery, causing flattening of the cornea and inducing hyperopia. If the surgeon chooses to make a corneal cataract incision, it should be placed between RK incisions. Violating an old RK incision can destabilize the wound. Multiple deep RK incisions increase the likelihood of anterior chamber shallowing during cataract surgery. Prior RK should not cause loss of the red reflex or affect the rate of cystoid macular edema.

pool.q: In addition to elongation and movement toward the bow region of the lens, what changes occur to lens epithelial cells during terminal differentiation?

options.a: a decrease in cell protein content and an increased dependence on glycolysis for energy
options.b: a decrease in cellular protein content and decreased dependence on glycolysis
options.c: a decreased dependence on glycolysis and an increase in cellular organelles
options.d: an increase in cell protein content and loss of organelles

pool.rationale: Terminal differentiation is a process by which a precursor cell that was formerly capable of cell division permanently leaves the cell cycle. In lens cells, terminal differentiation involves elongation of the lens epithelial cells into lens fibers. This change is associated with a tremendous increase in the mass of cellular proteins in the fiber cell membrane. The cells lose organelles, including nuclei, mitochondria, and ribosomes. The loss of cell organelles is optically advantageous; however, the cells then become more dependent on glycolysis for energy production and become less active metabolically.

pool.q: What complication of cataract surgery is more common in patients with retinitis pigmentosa?
pool.rationale: Retinitis pigmentosa is a risk factor for the development of CME after cataract surgery. Additionally, retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is a risk factor for insufficient zonular support. RP is not associated with an increased risk of corneal edema, refractive surprise, or intraoperative floppy iris syndrome.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Lens & Cataract — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What preoperative condition can interfere with both preoperative IOL measurements and postoperative healing?
pool.rationale:
Keratoconjunctivitis sicca can prevent accurate preoperative keratometry and thus make accurate IOL selection difficult. This is especially important in patients considering toric or multifocal lenses. In addition, keratoconjunctivitis sicca may be associated with collagen vascular disease, rheumatoid arthritis, or Sjögren syndrome, which may prevent routine postoperative healing.
Patients with AMD should be counseled that they might not achieve 20/20 vision after cataract surgery. Patients with pseudoexfoliation are at higher risk for complications related to a weak zonule. Some IOL formulas are less accurate in the setting of high hyperopia.

pool.q: An ophthalmologist is performing phacoemulsification surgery on a patient with a dense, brunescent cataract. What nuclear disassembly technique would be the most likely to result in complications such as zonular stress or endothelial damage?
pool.rationale: In eyes with dense, brunescent cataracts, surgical manipulation increases the risks of iris trauma, zonular tearing, capsular rupture, vitreous loss, and the dropping of lens fragments into the posterior segment. The increased ultrasound energy required for phacoemulsification of dense lenses increases the risk of endothelial trauma and wound burn. Mechanical segmentation techniques for nucleus disassembly, such as vertical and horizontal chopping, require less ultrasound energy and may induce less zonular stress than the “divide and conquer” method.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Lens & Cataract — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: The patient shown in the photo is at increased risk for what complication following cataract surgery?
pool.rationale:
The patient in the photograph has rosacea and blepharitis. Blepharitis is a risk factor for post-cataract endophthalmitis and should be identified and treated preoperatively. Oily rings of debris around the lashes ("collarettes") are the hallmark of blepharitis and meibomianitis. Additional findings include congestion of the eyelid margins, plugging of the meibomian gland orifices, and frothy discharge on the lid margin. Patients with acne rosacea have erythema, telangiectasias, papules, rhinophyma, and pustules distributed over the cheeks, chin, forehead, and nose. Patients with these features of inflammation are at greater risk of endophthalmitis.
Corneal edema, retinal detachment, and ptosis are all possible postoperative complications of cataract surgery but are not associated with blepharitis.

pool.q: What is characteristic of the diagnosis or treatment of clinical cystoid macular edema (CME) following cataract extraction?

options.a: Cystoid macular edema responds only to systemic nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents (NSAIDs), since it is posterior.
options.b: Cystoid macular edema was common (40% to 70%) following intracapsular cataract extraction (ICCE), but the incidence is less than 0.1% with the phacoemulsification technique.
options.c: Cystoid macular edema can only be diagnosed by fluorescein angiography, since there are no consistent retinal foveal changes.
options.d: Cystoid macular edema is seen more frequently in cases that have vitreomacular traction.

pool.rationale:
The prevalence of clinically apparent cystoid macular edema following cataract extraction is 1.2% to 3.5% of cases. Although the pathogenesis of CME is unknown, the final common pathway appears to be increased capillary permeability with accumulation of fluid in the inner nuclear and outer plexiform layers of the retina. CME is often associated with intraocular inflammation and may be mediated through the release of prostaglandins and leukotrienes. Associated intraoperative risk factors include vitreomacular traction, excessive exposure to ultraviolet (UV) light, posterior capsule rupture, vitreous loss, iris prolapse, and transient or prolonged hypotony.
Clinically apparent cystoid macular edema is defined in contrast to angiographic CME. Angiographic CME occurs in 40% to 70% of eyes following ICCE and in approximately 1% to 19% following extracapsular cataract extraction (ECCE) via nuclear expression or phacoemulsification, and is visible on fluorescein angiography, but not by traditional ophthalmoscopy. Clinically apparent CME can be recognized by the characteristic petaloid appearance of cystic spaces in the macula on ophthalmoscopy and by fluorescein angiography, or by cystic areas of low reflectivity and retinal thickening on spectral domain OCT.
The risk of CME may be reduced with preoperative and postoperative prophylactic use of topical ketorolac or other NSAID eyedrops. Because most cases of postoperative CME resolve spontaneously, it is difficult to assess the effect of these therapeutic agents. In a prospective randomized controlled clinical trial, topical ketorolac 0.5% or prednisolone acetate 1.0% was demonstrated to be effective therapy for chronic CME, but greater improvement in visual acuity was obtained with a combination of ketorolac and prednisolone 4 times per day than with either medication alone. Systemic NSAIDs have not been demonstrated to be effective therapy.

pool.q: What management strategy may be employed to reduce risk of intraoperative or postoperative uveal effusion for cataract surgery on a nanophthalmic eye?

options.c: lowering infusion pressure (eg, lower irrigation bottle height)

pool.rationale:
Nanophthalmos is a rare condition in which the eye is extremely short (axial length <20.5 mm) and the ratio of lens volume to eye volume is larger than normal. These eyes have shallow anterior chambers, narrow angles, and thickened sclerae, with little room for the surgeon to maneuver. Small-incision bimanual surgery is an alternative technique to consider. Intraoperative or postoperative uveal effusion is a unique hazard in nanophthalmic eyes. Maintaining positive pressure in the anterior chamber and limiting the length of the procedure aid in preventing intraoperative uveal effusion.
Scleral windows, not additional paracentesis incisions, should be considered as a prophylactic measure to treat uveal effusion. A sutured wound prevents hypotony from contributing to this complication postoperatively.
Other maneuvers, such as elevation of the irrigation bottle and making anterior corneal incisions to minimize iris prolapse, are recommended.

pool.q: A patient with complaints of negative dysphotopsia following otherwise uneventful cataract surgery is referred to an ophthalmologist. What is associated with this patient's symptom?
pool.rationale:
Negative dysphotopsia is described as an arcuate dark or dim crescent-shaped region, usually in the temporal visual field. It occurs in the setting of a posterior chamber intraocular lens (PCIOL) centered in the capsular bag with the anterior capsule edge overlapping the lens optic. Though reported with most styles of PCIOLs, negative dysphotopsia is more common with smaller, square-edge optic designs. Temporal light rays may interact with the nasal lens edge and anterior capsule, causing a shadow (penumbra) on the nasal retina in susceptible eyes. This effect is more common with a miotic or nasally located pupil and is relieved with dilation or by blocking light from the temporal side.
Although symptoms are common in the early postoperative period, they improve over time in most patients, presumably as the capsule contracts or opacifies in the periphery. Initially, observation is advised. For patients with prolonged symptoms and compromised vision, surgery may be necessary. Repositioning of the optic anterior to the capsulorrhexis by reverse optic capture through the capsulorrhexis (with the haptics in the capsular bag) or sulcus fixation of an appropriate PCIOL with a larger optic with rounded edges may be successful in most cases. Implanting a piggyback IOL or performing an anterior capsulectomy has been successful in some cases.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Lens & Cataract — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What complication is most likely to occur if there is intravitreal retained lens material?
pool.rationale: Corectopia, hypopyon, and hypotony are not sequelae of retained lens material. Reported complications of retained lens material are corneal edema, prolonged inflammation, secondary glaucoma, cystoid macular edema, and retinal detachment.

pool.q: If a patient has mild glaucoma and has a visually significant cataract, what is the average amount of intraocular pressure (IOP)-lowering effect that may be expected from performing phacoemulsification and IOL implantation on an eye with high IOP?
pool.rationale: Uncomplicated phacoemulsification surgery has been shown to lower IOP between 10% and 34%, on average, in some eyes. It can therefore be considered as a stand-alone procedure in eyes with early to moderate glaucoma. For more advanced cases of glaucoma and visually significant cataract, adjunctive filtration procedures may need to be considered at the time of cataract surgery. Staged procedures can also be considered (either cataract or glaucoma procedure first, then second procedure at later date). Factors to consider when deciding types and order of procedures include IOP goal, level of severity of glaucoma/visual field damage, patient adherence, side effects/number of medications, and effect on quality of life.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Lens & Cataract — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What systemic medication is most likely to cause severe intraoperative floppy iris syndrome (IFIS)?
pool.rationale: Tamsulosin is a selective α1a-adrenergic antagonist commonly prescribed to treat lower urinary tract symptoms associated with benign prostatic hypertrophy. Selective α1a-adrenergic antagonists have a greater effect on the iris dilator muscle than do nonselective agents. Alfuzosin is a nonselective α-adrenergic antagonist used to treat prostatic hypertrophy and is less likely to cause the same degree of IFIS as the selective α1a medications. Doxazosin and terazosin are also nonselective α-adrenergic antagonists; they are used to treat hypertension or prostatic hypertrophy.

pool.q: If an attempted continuous curvilinear capsulorrhexis has extended peripherally, what management technique should be applied?

options.a: enlarging the wound to aid in grasping the capsule
options.b: deepening of the anterior chamber and flattening of the capsule flap with viscoelastic
options.d: lowering pressure within the eye by removing viscoelastic

pool.rationale:
Maintaining the continuity of a continuous curvilinear capsulorrhexis is paramount to retaining its primary advantage of reducing the risk of tears extending to the posterior capsule during phacoemulsification. Any factor that causes shallowing of the anterior chamber will result in the lens moving forward, which would encourage extension of the capsule tear outward during creation of the capsulorrhexis. Ophthalmic viscosurgical devices (OVDs) should be added to hold the lens back and depress the anterior capsular surface, relieving outward tension on the peripheral anterior capsule by the anterior zonular apparatus.
Aspirating OVDs or enlarging or depressing the wound or the globe will encourage expulsion of OVDs and allow forward movement of the lens and outward pressure on the capsule. Even lightly depressing the central lens posteriorly with an instrument inserted through a sideport incision may also help reduce outward radialization of the tear and allow better inward control.
After maintaining the lens apparatus deeply and posteriorly with OVDs, the most common technique for maximally controlling the tear inward is to regrasp the flap near the end of the tear and slowly re-curve it inward.
An additional innovative technique has been recently described: The flap near the tear terminus is allowed to lie back down in its original position, then the flap is grabbed near the tear terminus and pulled slowly and gently back, as if to be lightly stretched back down into its original position and slightly inward, which will usually result in an abrupt inward turn of the tear.
Conversion to can-opener technique is reasonable, but an attempt should be made to redirect the continuous tear first, due to the increased risk of extension with a can-opener rhexis.

pool.q: A 52-year-old man with Marfan syndrome is scheduled for cataract extraction. At his preoperative examination 2 months earlier, the lens was found to be centered and stable. However, on the day of surgery, the lens is subluxated. What surgical adjunct may be considered to avoid lens dislocation?
pool.rationale:
The preoperative discovery of a subluxated crystalline lens compels the surgeon to consider means by which the remaining zonules can be supported and augmented. Early in the procedure, the surgeon should provide additional zonule support with a capsule support hook system.
Malyugin ring and intracameral epinephrine are most often used to manage a miotic pupil, which does not specifically apply to a luxated crystalline lens. Trypan blue improves visualization of the capsule contrasted against a densely opacified lens, which is not described as a feature of the above-described clinical case.

pool.q: What molecular activity in the crystalline lens is most associated with the development of age-related nuclear sclerosis?

options.a: Intermediate filaments form from the proteins vimentin, phakinin, and filensin.
options.b: ß-Crystallins associate with each other to form dimers and higher-order complexes.
options.c: Protein-to-glutathione disulfide bond formation results in increased protein aggregation.
options.d: a-Crystallins bind to partially denatured proteins and prevent them from aggregating.

pool.rationale:
Cataract formation occurs as proteins aggregate to become very large particles that are water-insoluble and scatter light. As a lens ages, associated oxidative changes lead to increased aggregation of proteins by protein-to-protein and protein-to-glutathione disulfide bond formation. Glutathione in its reduced form is seen as an essential antioxidant (to maintain a reducing environment in the lens cytoplasm). When it is depleted by protein-to-glutathione disulfide bond formation, there is accelerated protein crosslinking, protein aggregation, and light scattering.
The other molecular events create the normal proteins that make up the human lens. The lens has at least twice the protein concentration of most other tissues (lens protein concentration: 33% of its wet weight). α-Crystallins are water soluble and represent one-third of the lens proteins. They bind to partially denatured proteins and prevent aggregation, thus inhibiting the complete denaturation and insolubilization of other crystallins.
The other water-soluble proteins are β,γ-Crystallins. Remember cataract formation is associated with increased water-insoluble proteins. β-Crystallins are encoded by 7 genes. Individual polypeptides associate with one another to form dimers and higher-order complexes in their native state. Intermediate filaments are part of the water-insoluble fraction of lens protein; however, they are one component of the structural framework of the lens cells. Thus they are not associated with cataract formation unless there is genetic disruption of their structure, in particular in the beaded filaments, which are composed of phakinin and filensin (proteins specific to the lens).
The other intermediate filament type aside from beaded filaments is one made from the protein vimentin, which is not usually seen in epithelial cells.

pool.q: On examination 9 months following routine uncomplicated cataract extraction, a patient with no prior ocular comorbidities presents with intraocular pressure of 32 mm Hg in the operative eye. Slit-lamp examination is significant for a gray retrocorneal opacification in proximity to the main wound, with associated corneal edema. No lens material is seen in the angle on gonioscopy. What is the most likely mechanism of elevated intraocular pressure in this patient?
pool.rationale:
The description of retrocorneal opacification with corneal edema following intraocular surgery is alluding to epithelial ingrowth (also called downgrowth), which is a rare condition characterized by a sheet of epithelium growing intraocularly following trauma or a surgical incision and covering the corneal endothelium, trabecular meshwork, and/or iris surfaces. One of the clinical signs of epithelial downgrowth is an elevated intraocular pressure (IOP). The mechanism for elevated IOP is outflow obstruction caused by the growth of the epithelial membrane over the trabecular meshwork or by epithelial cells clogging the meshwork.
Retained ophthalmic viscosurgical device is a common cause for elevated IOP following cataract surgery, but usually peaks 4 to 6 hours following surgery, and is more typical with higher viscosity agents. Postoperative inflammation is an unlikely mechanism, given that the patient is 9 months out from surgery and the examination does not demonstrate significant anterior chamber inflammation. Posterior misdirection of aqueous is the classically described mechanism for malignant glaucoma or aqueous misdirection, in which secondary angle-closure glaucoma results from anterior rotation of the ciliary body, with resultant posterior misdirection of aqueous humor into the vitreous cavity. Another cause of elevated IOP following cataract surgery is retained anterior chamber or posterior chamber lens material, although in the scenario depicted in the question stem, the result of the gonioscopic examination was negative.

pool.q: What is a benefit of implanting the secondary piggyback intraocular lens (IOL) in the ciliary sulcus compared to in the capsular bag?

options.c: less risk of postoperative intraocular pressure elevation
options.d: decreased incidence of pupillary optic capture with mydriasis

pool.rationale: With secondary piggyback IOL implantation, the secondary IOL can be implanted in the ciliary sulcus or in the capsular bag. One benefit of ciliary sulcus implantation of the IOL is decreased incidence of interlenticular opacification. Postoperative elevation of intraocular pressure is associated with both locations of secondary IOL. Both methods can be used to correct postoperative astigmatism. Pupillary optic capture is more likely with sulcus IOL placement.

pool.q: After laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) is performed on a myopic patient, how will the central corneal power differ when measured by a standard keratometer compared to determination with corneal topography?

options.a: Corneal curvature may be significantly greater with either measure depending upon the degree of myopia.
options.b: Corneal curvature is underestimated by keratometry compared to topography.
options.c: Corneal curvature is overestimated by keratometry compared to topography.
options.d: Mean corneal curvature measurements will be within 0.25 D of each other.

pool.rationale: Because of post-LASIK corneal curvature changes, the central cornea tends to be less curved than the annular surrounding area. Therefore, standard keratometry, which measures corneal curvature over the central 3 mm, measures the corneal curvature to be greater than the topographic measure or refractive equivalent. Because of this effect, if a standard keratoscopic reading is used later to estimate the power for an intraocular lens, this may result in a refractive surprise.

pool.q: What intraocular lens (IOL) scenario increases the risk of uveitis-glaucoma-hyphema (UGH) syndrome?

options.c: implantation of an anterior chamber intraocular lens (ACIOL) oriented with posterior vault

pool.q: What is the greatest risk factor for retinal detachment after cataract surgery?
pool.rationale: The risk of retinal detachment is less than 1.0% following phacoemulsification. Axial myopia (>25 mm) carries the greatest risk of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RRD). pool.q: What intraoperative/postoperative condition may occur in a patient with high hyperopia during cataract surgery?

pool.q: What best describes viscosity as a physical property of an ophthalmic viscosurgical device (OVD)?

options.a: degree to which its surface sticks to another surface
options.b: ease with which it can be irrigated out of the eye
options.c: resistance to flow; the thickness and thinness of a fluid
options.d: ability to return to its original shape after being stressed

pool.rationale:
Viscosity is resistance to flow and can be thought of as the “thickness” or “thinness” of a fluid. It is determined primarily by molecular weight and concentration, so that substances with high molecular weight and high concentration have the highest viscosity. The higher the viscosity, the better the OVD is at displacing tissue and staying in place.
Elasticity refers to the ability of a material to return to its original shape after being stressed. It describes the OVD’s ability to re‑form after an external force is applied to the anterior chamber and then removed.
Surface tension describes how the surface of a fluid tends to stick to another surface. This property is also referred to as coatability, which is inversely proportional to surface tension. Thus, an OVD with low surface tension is better at coating tissue but is harder to remove from the eye.
Cohesive OVDs are long-chain, high-molecular-weight, high-viscosity substances. These agents maintain space well at no or low shear rates, whereas at high shear rates they are easily displaced. Cohesive OVDs are easier to remove from the eye because they stick together and are aspirated as long pieces (similar to spaghetti). However, they have minimal coating ability and therefore afford less tissue protection during surgery.

pool.q: What postoperative complication may occur with excessive stretching of the iris to improve dilation during cataract surgery?

pool.q: What are the characteristics of positive dysphotopsias from intraocular lenses (IOLs)?

pool.q: A patient with a history of herpes simplex virus (HSV)-1 positive recurrent hypertensive anterior uveitis has a visually significant cataract in the affected eye. The eye has not been inflamed for over 4 months. What management prior to cataract surgery should be performed to ensure the least chance of having a recurrence of inflammation postoperatively?

What should the ophthalmologist recommend ?

pool.q: What type of cataract is associated with chalcosis?
pool.rationale:
Chalcosis occurs when an intraocular foreign body deposits copper in the Descemet membrane, anterior lens capsule, or other intraocular basement membranes. The term sunflower cataract refers to a ­petal-­shaped deposition of yellow or brown pigment in the lens capsule that radiates from the anterior axial pole of the lens to the equator.
Oil-droplet cataracts can occur in galactosemia and posterior lenticonus, and the term is used to describe some dense nuclear cataracts. The oil-droplet appearance of dense nuclear cataracts in galactosemia is due to a great difference between the density of the central nucleus and that of the surrounding cortex. The oil-droplet appearance noted on red reflex exam in cases of posterior lenticonus is due to a bulge in the posterior capsule. In all these cases, the best way to view the oil droplet is with retinoscopy or with direct ophthalmoscopy using a ­wide-­angle view.
While posterior capsular cataracts are one of the main types of cataract related to aging, they can also occur as a result of trauma; systemic, topical, or intraocular corticosteroid use; inflammation; exposure to ionizing radiation; and prolonged alcohol abuse.
Anterior subcapsular cataracts occur with aging, ionizing radiation, electrical injuries, and atopic dermatitis.

Malignant hyperthermia more commonly develops under general anesthesia than with conscious sedation, so general anesthesia should be avoided. pool.q: During cataract extraction with IOL implantation in an 80-year-old patient, a "stop and chop" technique is used to remove the first half of the lens nucleus. The surgeon then notices a posterior capsular tear, and immediately the remaining half of the lens nucleus falls into the vitreous cavity. What management is recommended next?

options.b: Add viscoelastic gel and then remove the phacoemulsification needle from the eye.
options.c: Remove the phacoemulsification needle from the eye.

pool.rationale:
After recognizing a posterior capsular tear, the surgeon's first step is to cease all phacoemulsification and aspiration. To avoid further complications, the anterior chamber should be stabilized by irrigating and placing a dispersive viscoelastic to prevent anterior movement of vitreous. The effect of these maneuvers will maintain a deep anterior chamber and prevent a net flow of vitreous from moving forward. Following the surprise of recognition of a capsular tear, the temptation to immediately remove all instruments from the eye must be avoided.
Removal of the phacoemulsification needle alone collapses and destabilizes the anterior chamber. Continued phacoemulsification or aspiration will likely engage vitreous and thereby apply traction to the retina. Vitreous tamponade, followed by management of remaining nucleus or cortex with an anterior vitrector, will be much more efficacious.

pool.q: For an elderly patient with dense nuclear sclerotic cataracts and severe blepharitis, what special considerations might be considered in view of the increased risk of postoperative endophthalmitis?

options.a: Plan for an extracapsular cataract extraction to minimize repeated manipulation of instruments in the eye and over the eyelashes.
options.b: Plan to use intravenous antibiotics in the irrigating solution.
options.c: Recommend eyelid hygiene to the patient and have the patient return for re-evaluation before surgery.
options.d: Plan to scrub the eyelids and lashes vigorously with 10% povidone-iodine soap on the day of surgery.

On the day of surgery, the use of 5% ­povidone-­iodine solution in the fornix has been shown to decrease bacterial colony counts. Systemic antibiotics do not adequately penetrate an intact globe. Although minimizing repeated manipulation of instruments over the eyelashes and in the eye is recommended, making a large incision for an extracapsular extraction is not advised. Appropriate eyelid hygiene preoperatively would be the recommended course of action in this case.

pool.q: An 83-year-old woman presents with an uncorrected visual acuity of 20/70. There is no significant improvement with the pinhole acuity test. pool.q: During hydrodissection, why is gentle posterior pressure applied on the central nucleus?

options.b: to separate the nucleus from the cortex
options.c: to break capsulorhexis-lenticular block and propagate the fluid wave
options.d: to facilitate nuclear disassembly during phacoemulsification of the nucleus

pool.rationale:
It is important to apply gentle posterior pressure centrally on the nucleus to prevent buildup of fluid posteriorly that can lead to rupture of the posterior capsule. Hydrodissection separates the peripheral cortex from the posterior capsule. It does not protect the corneal endothelium or facilitate nuclear disassembly.

Hydrodissection is performed to separate the peripheral and posterior cortex from the underlying posterior lens capsule. In addition to loosening the lens–cortex complex, this procedure facilitates nucleus rotation during phacoemulsification and hydrates the peripheral cortex, making it easier to aspirate after nucleus removal. In this procedure, the surgeon places a bent, blunt-tipped 25- to 30-gauge cannula or flattened hydrodissection cannula attached to a 3- to 5-mL syringe under the anterior capsule flap. While carefully lifting the capsular flap, the surgeon injects balanced salt solution in a radial direction. Exerting gentle posterior pressure on the nucleus will express posterior fluid and prevent fluid pressure from rupturing the posterior capsule. Gentle irrigation continues until the surgeon sees a wave of fluid moving under the nucleus and across the red reflex. In mature cataracts or in cases without a red reflex, careful hydrodissection continues until nucleus rotation can be performed. Irrigation in the subincisional area may require a right-angled or J-shaped hydrodissection cannula.

pool.q: What would have been the best course of action during cataract surgery to prevent the postoperative finding shown in the photo?

Often times, a thin refractile line can be seen, corresponding to the transition zone between detached and attached Descemet membrane. For large or central detachments (such as the one shown), intracameral air or expansile gas can help reattach the DM. Sometimes sutures are required to reattach the DM.
An anterior vitrectomy would be needed for vitreous in the anterior chamber; however, there is not peaking of the pupil to suggest the abnormal light reflex is part of the vitreous.

pool.q: What is the most active pathway for glucose metabolism in the lens?
pool.rationale:
Energy production within the lens depends on the metabolism of glucose, which enters the lens through simple and facilitated diffusion from the aqueous humor. The glucose is phosphorylated to glucose-6-phosphate (G6P) by hexokinase before being transferred into the lens, and this is the rate-limiting step of glucose metabolism in the lens. Anaerobic glycolysis utilizes about 80% of glucose processes for energy in the lens. Less than 4% is normally converted to sorbitol. Less than 5% is metabolized by the HMP pathway. Only about 3% of the lens glucose passes through the Krebs cycle; however, even this low level of aerobic metabolism produces approximately 25% of the ATP of the lens. One glucose molecule will create 2 adenosine triphosphate (ATP) molecules via anaerobic glycolysis.
Under conditions of very high concentrations of sugar, the sorbitol pathway is activated, converting glucose to sorbitol and then fructose. This pathway then competes with anaerobic glycolysis for glucose. Aldose reductase is the enzyme in this pathway that converts glucose to sorbitol, and it is activated only when glucose concentrations are very high. Therefore, "sugar cataracts" are thought to develop when high concentrations of glucose activate aldose reductase, which increases the lens concentration of sorbitol. Sorbitol then osmotically drives water into the lens and causes cataract formation.
The hexose monophosphate shunt (pentose phosphate shunt) is activated under times of oxidative stress because it replenishes nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NAPDH), which is oxidized by the glutathione reductase pathway in times of oxidative stress. Only 3% of the glucose is metabolized directly by the Krebs cycle. Pyruvate is the major substrate used for ATP production by the Krebs cycle.

pool.q: What intraoperative adjustment should be made if excessive postocclusion surge is noticed during cataract surgery?

options.a: Change to a wider-gauge phaco needle.

pool.rationale: Postocclusion surge is caused when the phacoemulsification needle tip, which has been occluded by lens material, becomes acutely exposed to fluid at high or maximum suction levels. Until the needle tip engages another lens fragment or the vacuum is lowered, the suction in a confined space may lead to a sudden collapse of the anterior chamber. The most useful maneuver to reduce or avoid the postocclusion surge is to reduce the maximum vacuum setting. The bottle height and the aspiration flow rate have lesser effects on reducing the surge magnitude. A narrower-lumen phaco needle that restricts flow, rather than a larger-lumen needle, will reduce postocclusion surge.

pool.q: As a human crystalline lens ages, how do its optical characteristics change?

options.a: There is an increase in the index of refraction as a result of the decreasing presence of insoluble protein particles.
options.b: There is a decrease in the index of refraction as a result of the decreasing presence of insoluble protein particles.
options.c: It develops an increasing anterior and posterior curvature, resulting in more refractive power.
options.d: It becomes increasingly flat, resulting in less refractive power.

pool.rationale: With age, the human lens develops an increasingly curved shape along the anterior and posterior surfaces, which results in more refractive power. This change can be accompanied by — and in some cases offset by — a decrease in the index of refraction of the lens, probably resulting from an increase in water-­insoluble proteins. As a result, either a myopic or hyperopic shift in refraction can occur. This contrasts with the increased index of refraction often seen in lenses with nuclear sclerosis.

pool.q: What diagnostic modality is most appropriate to perform prior to cataract surgery in a patient with opaque media that is preventing an adequate view into the eye?
pool.rationale: B-scan ultrasonography of the posterior segment of the eye is useful whenever a dense cataract or opaque media makes visualization of the retina impossible. It can elucidate whether a retinal detachment, vitreous opacity, posterior pole tumor, or staphyloma is present. Biometry, whether it be ultrasonography or optical coherence biometry, is used to measure the axial length of the eye for intraocular lens (IOL) calculations. Indirect biomicroscopy is unlikely to provide an adequate view with significantly opaque media.

pool.q: What factor may reduce posterior capsular opacification following implantation of an acrylic foldable IOL?

options.d: capsulorrhexis larger than the unfolded lens optic

pool.rationale: Use of a truncated or square-edge optic design decreases the incidence of posterior capsular opacification (PCO). Such an optic is thought to exert a mechanical barrier effect, create contact inhibition of migrating lens epithelial cells (LECs) at the capsular bend, and exert higher pressures on the posterior capsule. These effects prevent growth and migration of LECs and thus reduce the incidence of PCO. A large capsulorrhexis increases wrinkling and opacification of the posterior capsule, which has been demonstrated in multiple studies. Avoiding hydrodissection of the cortex makes cortical clean-up more difficult, which likely increases the risk of PCO. Ciliary sulcus placement of the IOL haptics increases risk and incidence of PCO.

pool.q: Where in the body can the fibrillar material of pseudoexfoliation be found?
pool.rationale: Exfoliation syndrome (pseudoexfoliation) is a systemic disease in which a matrix of fibrotic material is deposited in many organs throughout the entire body. In the eye, a basement membrane-like fibrillogranular white material is deposited on the lens, cornea, iris, anterior hyaloid face, ciliary processes, zonular fibers, and trabecular meshwork. Exfoliation syndrome is a unilateral or bilateral disorder that becomes more apparent with increasing age.

pool.q: The lens has higher levels of what, compared to the surrounding aqueous and vitreous?
pool.rationale:
+

The lens has higher concentrations of K+ and amino acids. As it is dehydrated, it has lower concentrations of H2O (remember that the lens swells when the capsule is violated). It also has lower concentrations of Na+ and Cl- compared to the surrounding aqueous and vitreous. Recall that the Na+/K+ ATPase is located on the anterior lens capsule and creates the gradient of elevated intralenticular K+ and elevated extralenticular Na+.

pool.q: During preoperative evaluation of a patient with a dense posterior subcapsular cataract, the ophthalmologist is unable to obtain a reliable optical biometry determination of axial length. What diagnostic modality is the most appropriate to use in this scenario?
pool.rationale:
Ocular axial length is a critical biometry measurement used in determining the appropriate power of an intraocular lens implant prior to cataract surgery. Optical biometers use optical coherence reflectometry to measure axial length, among other parameters; however, they are not foolproof and may not be reliable in the setting of corneal scarring and media opacities such as mature cataracts and vitreous hemorrhage. In those scenarios, A-scan ultrasonography can be used to measure axial length, using either an immersion or applanation technique.
Ultrasound biomicroscopy, anterior segment optical coherence tomography, and orbital computed tomography would not provide a reliable axial length measurement for cataract surgery planning.

pool.q: Following the prepping and draping for cataract surgery, the ophthalmologist applies topical 4% lidocaine, but the patient repeatedly squeezes his eye, which dislodges the lid speculum entirely. The surgeon then undrapes the patient and performs a local anesthetic block of the terminal branches of the facial nerve, inserting the needle 1 cm inferior and lateral to the lateral canthus. What is the name of this procedure?
pool.rationale: The van Lint block is performed on the terminal branches just temporal to the lateral canthus. The Nadbath-Ellis block targets CN VII trunk as it exits the stylomastoid foramen between the mastoid process and the posterior border of the mandibular ramus. The O'Brien block targets CN VII just anterior to the tragus at the condyloid process of the mandible. The Atkinson block targets the temporofacial branch of CN VII by anesthetizing a path from the inferior border of the zygoma, passing superiorly across the zygomatic arch toward the top of the ear.

pool.q: What in-office clinical test may aid in testing macular function in a patient with a dense cataract that precludes visualization of the fundus?
pool.rationale:
In patients with dense cataracts that preclude adequate visualization of the fundus preoperatively, Maddox rod testing aids in evaluating macular function. Any large scotoma, represented as a loss of the red line of the Maddox glass as viewed by the patient, should raise the possibility of significant macular disease. Tests such as light projection, 2-point discrimination, gross color vision, photostress recovery, or blue-light entoptoscopy, may also be useful in detecting retinal pathology and would have been good answers to this question. Electroretinography and visually evoked response testing are warranted when other modalities are inconclusive and the surgeon must decide whether cataract removal would provide any benefit.
Amsler grid testing is of course useful for testing for the central 20° of visual field. The optokinetic (OKN) drum can be used to evaluate saccades and pursuit. It is also valuable in evaluation of functional vision loss.
After an episode of demyelinating optic neuritis, a relative conduction delay within the affected optic nerve may lead to an altered perception of motion. Because of the disparity in neuronal transmission, a pendulum, for example, may appear to trace an elliptical path instead of its true single-plane oscillation. This is known as the Pulfrich phenomenon.

pool.q: What type of cataract is associated with atopic dermatitis?
pool.rationale:
Atopic dermatitis is a chronic, erythematous dermatitis, accompanied by itching and often seen in conjunction with increased levels of immunoglobulin E and a history of multiple allergies or asthma. Cataract formation has been reported in up to 25% of patients with atopic dermatitis. The cataracts are usually bilateral, and onset occurs in the second to third decade of life. Typically, these cataracts are anterior subcapsular opacities in the pupillary area that resemble shieldlike plaques.
Cortical and nuclear sclerotic cataracts have nonspecific or multiple causes. Anterior polar cataracts are typically congenital.

pool.q: What intraoperative finding is common in eyes undergoing removal of a posterior polar cataract?
pool.rationale: In a posterior polar cataract, there is a weak or absent area of posterior lens capsule in the area of the posterior polar opacity. As a result, there is an increased risk of capsular rupture during cataract surgery. There is no increased risk of weak zonules or shallow chamber. A poor red reflex is also not more common in a posterior polar cataract.

pool.q: What enzyme plays a pivotal role in the development of "sugar" cataracts?
pool.rationale: In hyperglycemic states, glucose accumulates and the sorbitol pathway is activated relatively more than the glycolytic pathway. In the sorbitol pathway, aldose reductase converts glucose to sorbitol. Hexokinase is inhibited as glycolysis products increase. Phosphofructokinase is not involved in the sorbitol pathway; rather, it is involved in anaerobic glycolysis. Lactic dehydrogenase also is not involved and it converts pyruvate to lactate.

pool.q: Following cataract surgery with posterior chamber intraocular lens (IOL) implantation in the capsular bag, a patient has glare and a vague shadow (double) image. Given the abnormalities shown, what is the most likely cause of this problem?
pool.rationale:
This patient has a subluxed IOL with a capsular tear extending from the 7:30 o'clock position. There are many causes of IOL decentration and dislocation, including:
  • asymmetric haptic placement with one haptic in the capsular bag and the other in the sulcus, or a tear in posterior capsule or capsular bag;
  • a broken or damaged haptic or IOL fixation suture;
  • an eccentric or a torn capsulorrhexis;
  • insufficient zonular support;
  • irregular fibrosis of the capsular bag;
  • or implantation of an IOL with insufficient haptic length in the ciliary sulcus.
Pseudoexfoliation would cause a dislocation of the entire IOL/capsule complex and would not explain the capsule defect. This is not a plate-haptic IOL. Asymmetric placement of the haptics cannot be diagnosed as the haptics are not seen in the figure.

Examination reveals that the IOL in the left eye is decentered; the margin of the capsulorrhexis crosses the optic nasally but extends beyond the edge of the optic temporally. pool.q: What is a clinical finding that can help distinguish toxic anterior segment syndrome (TASS) from infectious endophthalmitis?

Corneal topography that evaluates corneal surface shape would not be helpful. While useful for many causes of corneal edema, specular microscopy best evaluates the central cornea that is not edematous, and it would not rule out the possibility of retained lens material. Macular OCT would not be revealing for this corneal condition.

pool.q: What is a modifiable risk factor for age-related cataract?
pool.rationale:
Smoking is an established risk factor for development of nuclear sclerotic cataract and posterior subcapsular cataract (PSC). The Beaver Dam Eye Study and the Blue Mountains Eye Study, among others, concluded that there is a higher and dose-related risk of visually significant nuclear sclerosis for study participants who smoke. Some smoking-related damage to the lens may be reversible upon cessation.
Additional risk factors for cataract identified by multiple studies include UV-light exposure, diabetes mellitus, prolonged corticosteroid use (systemic, inhaled, and topical), ocular trauma (including prior ocular surgery), and high myopia. Also implicated in the development of cataract are exogenous estrogen use, alcohol consumption, and increased body mass index; however, study results regarding the impact of these factors are inconsistent.
The role of nutrition in preventing cataracts (specifically, the potential benefit of supplementation with antioxidants) has been a subject of recent interest. Some studies have shown a benefit to increased intake of vitamins C and E. However, in the Age-Related Eye Disease Study 1 (AREDS1), a formulation of vitamin C, vitamin E, beta carotene, zinc, and copper did not reduce the risk of progression to cataract surgery. In a large Italian trial, use of a multivitamin and mineral supplement benefited individuals with nuclear sclerotic cataract but increased the risk of PSC. The Age-Related Eye Disease Study 2 (AREDS2), results of which were published in 2013, evaluated the effects of lutein/zeaxanthin supplementation. This study concluded that these supplements had no significant overall effect on rates of progression to cataract surgery, although patients in the lowest quintile of dietary lutein/zeaxanthin intake did have a reduced risk of cataract development following supplementation.

pool.q: For a patient being evaluated for cataract surgery, what test can be useful in assessing the contribution of lenticular opacities to vision loss?
pool.rationale:
The potential acuity meter projects a numerical or Snellen vision chart through a small entrance pupil. The image can be projected onto the retina, around lenticular opacities, allowing for an estimate of what the best corrected visual acuity would be if the lens abnormality were absent. These tests can be misleading in the presence of several disorders, including age-related macular degeneration, amblyopia, macular edema, glaucoma, small macular scars, and serous retinal detachment. An accurate clinical eye exam is often the best predictor of visual outcome.
The Maddox rod test is for strabismus. Corneal topography is a useful test prior to cataract surgery, but not specifically to assess lenticular contribution of vision loss. Purkinje entoptic phenomenon is not a test of visual potential, but a phenomenon of entoptic images cast on the retina.

pool.q: A diabetic patient has cataract surgery that is complicated by capsular rupture and vitreous loss and requires conversion to extracapsular cataract extraction. One month later, the patient has decreased visual acuity and foreign body sensation. Examination reveals elevated intraocular pressure (IOP), corneal edema, abnormal iris surface, and an irregular pupil. What is the most likely diagnosis?

As a result, clinical features include elevated IOP, clumps of cells in the anterior chamber, a retrocorneal membrane, corneal edema, abnormal iris surface, and pupillary distortion. pool.q: What intervention is most likely to reduce the risk of microscope-induced light toxicity?

options.a: use of a coaxial light path
options.c: addition of a 600 nm wavelength filter to the microscope

pool.rationale: The primary method to reduce intraoperative light toxicity is to reduce the time and intensity of exposure to the blue and near-ultraviolet light end of the spectrum. This can be done by reducing operating time (specifically the time in which the operating microscope is allowed to illuminate the pupil). Filters have been installed in most ophthalmic operating microscopes to reduce blue to near-ultraviolet light. Filtering in the red or orange portion of the spectrum (ie, 600 nm) will not reduce retinal light toxicity. Coaxial light tends to increase the likelihood of toxicity; side illumination tends to reduce toxicity.

pool.q: What is the primary purpose of using a capsular tension ring during cataract surgery?

options.a: It allows sulcus fixation of an intraocular lens (IOL).
options.b: It provides capsular tension for adequate posterior capsular polishing.
options.c: It reduces the postoperative incidence of retinal detachment or retinal tear.
options.d: It stabilizes the capsular bag in the presence of zonular dialysis.

pool.rationale: The primary purpose of using an endocapsular ring during cataract surgery is to provide greater capsule stability in eyes where pre-existing zonular disruption is known to be present. Capsule stability allows more of these eyes to undergo successful in-the-bag IOL placement with small-incision phacoemulsification surgery. It is not used primarily for polishing the posterior capsule nor reducing the postoperative incidence of retinal detachment or tear.

pool.q: What medical therapy is contraindicated in the setting of corneal melting with ocular surface disease following cataract surgery?

This may be due to both direct epithelial toxicity and possible induced corneal hypoesthesia. Frequent use of preservative-free lubricants is a primary medical modality use to manage keratolysis.  Topical acetylcysteine is also an appropriate medical therapy and is used for its properties as a collagenase inhibitor. Topical antibiotics may be indicated for prophylaxis but their use should be monitored closely, because many topical antibiotics are associated with eventual corneal epithelial toxicity.

pool.q: What is a benefit of retrobulbar anesthesia compared to peribulbar anesthesia?

options.a: decreased time to administer the injections
options.b: increased patient comfort with the injection
options.c: decreased risk of optic nerve injury

pool.rationale: The onset of the anesthetic effect is more rapid with retrobulbar anesthesia than with peribulbar anesthesia. Retrobulbar anesthesia also provides more effective akinesia and anesthesia than does peribulbar anesthesia. With peribulbar anesthesia, the risk of optic nerve injury is decreased because a shorter needle is used. Conjunctival hemorrhage can be seen with both methods of anesthesia delivery. Both methods provide good anesthesia for patient comfort in most cases. The discomfort with the injections themselves is similar for patients, and there may be benefit to systemic sedation for the injections if practical. The time to administer the injections is similar for both types of anesthesia. For the most part, the preference of the surgeon dictates which type of anesthesia is used.

pool.q: What is the best management strategy for the appearance of multiple glistening deposits within the optic of a hydrophobic acrylic intraocular lens (IOL) in a patient with good visual acuity following cataract surgery?

pool.q: What complications may result from excessive ultrasound power and time during phacoemulsification?

pool.q: Following routine cataract surgery, a patient develops sterile corneal melting. What is the best first-line surgical management?
pool.rationale:
Corneal melting after cataract surgery is usually associated with preexisting keratoconjunctivitis sicca or Sjögren syndrome. It can be worsened by the use of preserved topical medications. Treatment is aimed at increasing the moisture and protecting the surface, primarily with liberal use of nonpreserved artificial tears. Surgical techniques such as lateral tarsorrhaphy and procedures such as punctal plug placement are also effective ways of increasing surface lubrication in these patients.
Some second- and third-line surgical management techniques include conjunctival or amniotic grafts, followed by lamellar and penetrating corneal grafts.
Excimer laser ablation is not a management strategy for corneal melting and could worsen the condition.
Application of an amniotic membrane corneal bandage without grafting has of late become easier and less expensive. Give yourself credit it you answered this in challenge mode.

pool.q: What technique helps maintain corneal clarity after cataract surgery in an eye that has previously undergone penetrating keratoplasty?

options.a: placing an anterior chamber intraocular lens
options.b: operating while corneal sutures are still in place

pool.rationale: A scleral tunnel approach minimizes endothelial injury during cataract surgery. It is also important to use adequate viscoelastic to protect the endothelium during surgery. Posterior chamber lenses are preferred because they minimize contact between the optic and the endothelium. Ideally, cataract surgery should be delayed until all penetrating keratoplasty sutures have been removed.

pool.q: What is the recommended initial management maneuver when a posterior capsule rupture during cataract surgery using phacoemulsification is suspected?

options.a: Remove all instruments and irrigation from the eye immediately.
options.b: Delay IOL placement until a retina surgeon removes any posterior lens fragments.
options.c: Enlarge the wound and convert to extracapsular cataract surgery.
options.d: Continue irrigation at foot position 1 and place dispersive ophthalmic viscoelastic gel into the anterior chamber.

pool.rationale: Once a ruptured posterior lens capsule is discovered, it is important to avoid anterior chamber collapse, which results in forward movement of the vitreous. The surgeon should immediately return to foot position 1. Before removing the phaco needle, the surgeon should instill a dispersive ophthalmic viscoelastic gel through a side port. The instruments should not be immediately removed as that might cause anterior chamber collapse and promote vitreous prolapse into the anterior chamber. While conversion to extracapsular surgery may be an option, it would not be an initial consideration after recognizing posterior capsular rupture. It is possible and usually preferable to place an IOL in a stable location even if a retina surgeon will later be removing lens fragments from the vitreous cavity.

pool.q: What complication is common in cataract surgery in a patient with nanophthalmos?

These eyes have shallow anterior chambers, narrow angles, and thickened sclerae, with little room for the surgeon to maneuver. Small-incision bimanual surgery is an alternative technique to consider. Maintaining positive pressure in the anterior chamber and limiting the length of the procedure aid in preventing intraoperative uveal effusion. pool.q: An 89-year-old glassblower presents for an annual examination with the anterior segment shown. What is the most likely cause of the condition of the anterior segment membrane?
pool.rationale:
Exposure of the glassblower's eye to infrared radiation and intense heat can cause the outer layers of the anterior capsule of the lens to peel and scroll up, similarly to the eye shown in the picture. When associated with a cortical cataract, these findings are referred to as a "glassblower's cataract."
Penetrating trauma is associated with cortical opacification at the site of rupture, which typically progresses to complete lens opacification but occasionally remains localized. Specific nutritional deficiencies associated with cataractogenesis have been difficult to confirm in human studies, although they are suggested by animal research. pool.q: A 70-year-old patient in the US presents with painless progressive decreased vision. The slit-lamp examination is shown. What is the most likely race and gender of the patient?
pool.rationale: The photo depicts a mature cortical cataract. Note the brighter white spokes or water clefts that stand out within a background of completely opaque lens cortex. pool.q: A 74-year-old patient complains of double vision, especially while driving, that has prevented her from night driving for 6 months. Her best-corrected vision is 20/40 OD and 20/30 OS. Her refraction is -1.50 +0.25 @ 90 OD and -0.75 +0.50 @ 75 OS. She notes that the diplopia resolves when covering her right eye, but persists when covering her left eye. She also notes that doubling of the chart letters resolves with pinhole viewing. Her lens examination is shown. Epiretinal membrane (ERM) can cause monocular diplopia, but this patient's ERMs are mild and symmetric. Prescription of prism in her glasses would not improve monocular diplopia. Irregular corneal astigmatism can cause monocular diplopia and would be improved with pinhole viewing. However, this patient’s refraction precludes this.

pool.q: What type of cataract is most commonly associated with corticosteroid use?
pool.rationale: Posterior subcapsular cataracts are one of the main types of cataracts related to aging; however, they can also occur as a result of corticosteroid use, trauma, inflammation, exposure to ionizing radiation, and alcoholism. The other types of cataracts listed (anterior polar cataract, posterior polar cataract, coronal cataract) are not associated with steroid use; they are some types of congenital/pediatric cataracts.

pool.q: One day after an uncomplicated cataract surgery, a patient has an intraocular pressure (IOP) of 55 mm Hg. She has a brow ache and has vomited 3 times. The cornea demonstrates microcystic edema and the anterior chamber is deep. What is the most appropriate next course of action?

options.a: Manually lower the pressure by pressing on the lip of the main incision.
options.b: Send the patient home with brimonidine, dorzolamide, and timolol.
options.d: Manually lower the pressure by pressing on the lip of the sideport incision.

pool.rationale:
An ophthalmic viscosurgical device (OVD) retained in the eye after cataract surgery is frequently responsible for early postoperative IOP elevation, which peaks 4 to 6 hours after surgery. The large molecules of the viscoelastic material can impair aqueous outflow through the trabecular meshwork. Even when all apparent OVD is removed from the anterior chamber, residual OVD, particularly dispersive agents, can lodge in the posterior chamber or behind the lens implant. All types of OVDs, but in particular the higher-viscosity agents, may cause the pressure to rise. IOP elevation usually does not last more than a few days and is amenable to medical treatment. The clinician may quickly manage marked IOP elevation in the early postoperative period by applying gentle pressure on the posterior lip of a preexisting paracentesis incision to release a small amount of aqueous humor. Topical and/or systemic pressure-lowering agents should also be administered, as IOP reduction after aqueous release is short-lived, with the IOP likely to rise again within 1 to 2 hours of the decompression.
An oral agent is unlikely to be useful in a patient who is vomiting. Releasing aqueous from the smaller sideport incision is safer than opening the main incision.

pool.q: How should the intraocular lens (IOL) power be adjusted for a sulcus-fixated lens with the optic captured posterior to the anterior capsulorhexis?

However, this plan must sometimes be changed, such as when a posterior capsular tear unexpectedly occurs. The IOL power necessary to achieve the same refractive result sometimes must be adjusted. If the haptics and optic are at the level of the sulcus, then the power of the IOL will have to be adjusted by using a -0.5 to -1.5 less than the calculated IOL power, depending on the power of the IOL. However, for an IOL with the optic captured in the capsulotomy, with the optic posterior to the anterior capsulotomy, no adjustment is necessary.

pool.q: What is an advantage of retrobulbar anesthesia over topical anesthesia in cataract surgery?

options.b: lower risk of injury to extraocular muscles

pool.rationale: Retrobulbar anesthesia provides excellent anesthesia and akinesia. Complications are uncommon but include injury to extraocular muscles and globe perforation. With topical anesthesia, patients do not experience akinesia. They have faster visual recovery. The chance of injury to the globe or muscles is eliminated.

pool.q: What bacterium is most commonly isolated from intraocular cultures from patients with cataract surgery-associated endophthalmitis?

pool.q: What has been shown to decrease the risk of developing post-cataract surgery endophthalmitis?

options.a: povidone-iodine solution in the conjunctival fornix prior to the start of surgery
options.b: intracameral vancomycin at the end of cataract surgery
options.d: prophylactic topical antibiotics after cataract surgery

pool.rationale:
The relationship of host flora and postcataract endophthalmitis is not fully understood. However, despite the evidence that colony-forming units of bacteria are inoculated into the anterior chamber during most cataract surgeries, postcataract endophthalmitis remains a rare and sporadic disorder. In the Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study, most patients with Staphylococcus epidermidis infection had identical isotypes isolated from adnexal and intraocular cultures.
Due in part to the rarity of endophthalmitis and the limitation of statistical methods, demonstration of prophylaxis by topical or intraocular antibiotics has remained controversial. In contrast, anterior vitrectomy has been convincingly demonstrated to be associated with an increased incidence of endophthalmitis. The Endophthalmitis Study Group of the European Society of Cataract and Refractive Surgeons found a decrease in endophthalmitis rates in patients given intracameral cefuroxime.

pool.q: What is the classic appearance of a cataract associated with hypocalcemia?

options.a: stellate-shaped reddish-brown pigment in the anterior lens capsule and subcapsular cortex
options.b: increasing opacity in the nucleus and deep cortex
options.c: iridescent opacities in anterior and posterior cortex separated from lens capsule by clear zone
options.d: abrupt onset of widespread superficial subcapsular lens opacities

pool.rationale:
Cataracts may occur in any condition that causes hypocalcemia. The cataract is typically focal iridescent opacities within the cortex. Other metabolic conditions known to cause cataract include diabetes mellitus, galactosemia, Wilson disease, and myotonic dystrophy. Young patients with poorly controlled diabetic mellitus may develop an acute diabetic cataract or snowflake cataract consisting of bilateral, multiple gray-white subcapsular opacities. Vacuoles and clefts are also common in the lens of a person with diabetes. As diabetic patients age, they develop age-related changes similar to those in patients without diabetes, except the changes occur at a faster rate.
Galactosemia is an autosomal recessive disease that results in a lack of production of glucose from galactose. It is due to one of 3 enzyme deficiencies: galactose 1-phosphate uridyltransferase, galactokinase, or UDP galactose 4-epimerase. The most commonly involved enzyme is galactose 1-phosphate uridyltransferase. Patients develop an accumulation of galactose in the lens that drives in water osmotically and causes an "oil droplet" cataract in the cortex on retroillumination. Other findings of this disease include hepatomegaly, malnutrition, jaundice, and intellectual deficiency.
Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disease of copper metabolism. A "sunflower cataract" is sometimes seen as a result of cuprous oxide deposition in the anterior lens capsule and cortex. Another finding of Wilson disease is a Kayser-Fleischer ring, which is a golden brown coloration of the Descemet membrane.
Myotonic dystrophy is an autosomal dominant condition causing generalized muscle weakness, cardiac conduction defects, and frontal balding. Patients may develop iridescent opacities in the lens cortex with posterior subcapsular cataract.

pool.q: Pseudophakic cystoid macular edema (CME) has been associated with what ocular medication?
pool.rationale:
Topical prostaglandin analogues, particularly latanoprost, have been associated with reversible cystoid macular edema (CME) in eyes that have undergone recent intraocular surgery, although a cause-and-effect relationship has not been established. The risk is believed to be greater in the absence of an intact posterior capsule. CME has also been associated with the use of topical epinephrine and dipivefrin for the treatment of aphakic glaucoma.
An association of CME with topical beta blockers has not been established. Although glaucoma medications may be associated with CME, at times the need to prevent elevation of IOP outweighs the risk of CME.
Intracameral lidocaine has not been shown to be associated with CME. Subconjunctival gentamicin has uncommonly been associated with retinal toxicity, but not CME, due to inadvertent penetration of the globe during periocular injection.
Intravitreal vascular endothelial growth factor inhibitors (such as bevacizumab) have been used with success to treat chronic CME cases that do not respond to conventional treatment.

options.b: glycosaminoglycan deposits in the lens cell bodies
options.c: posterior migration of lens epithelial cells

pool.rationale: Posterior migration of lens epithelial cells and their enlargement are the typical histologic changes associated with PSCs. Lamellar membrane whorls are seen on electron microscopy of nuclear cataracts. Calcium deposition is seen in hypermature cataracts. Glycosaminoglycan deposition is not a feature of cataracts.

pool.q: An 83-year-old woman presents with a red, painful right eye. Examination of the involved eye reveals hand-movement vision, intraocular pressure of 36 mm Hg, mild corneal edema, open angle, white flocculent material in the anterior chamber, and mature cataract. What would definitive treatment consist of?

pool.q: An ophthalmologist leaves the room to scrub before beginning cataract surgery. Several minutes later, before the surgeon finishes scrubbing, the anesthesiologist reports that the patient is now unresponsive, apneic, and hypotensive. This complication is most likely a result of use of what route of ocular anesthetic?
pool.rationale: The patient’s central nervous system (CNS) and respiratory depression in this scenario are suggestive of brainstem anesthesia. Although rare, inadvertent intradural injection is possible with a retrobulbar block, and can lead to loss of consciousness, apnea, bradycardia, and hypotension, which can be fatal if unrecognized. Peribulbar, sub-Tenon, and topical anesthesia are not associated with intradural anesthesia.
