pool.q: What condition is most commonly associated with late dislocation of an intraocular lens (IOL) placed in the capsular bag?

options.a: previous surgery for chronic open-angle glaucoma

pool.rationale: The most common cause of intracapsular IOL dislocation is zonular degradation associated with pseudoexfoliation syndrome. Insufficient zonular support may also be due to trauma, previous vitreoretinal surgery (though not glaucoma surgery), capsular contraction, retinitis pigmentosa, high myopia, uveitis, or other congenital conditions affecting zonular integrity that are not corneal conditions.

pool.q: For patients undergoing cataract surgery, a history of what type of corneal refractive surgery is associated with a transitory hyperopic shift immediately after surgery?
pool.rationale: Patients who have had radial keratotomy commonly have a transitory hyperopic shift immediately after cataract surgery, due to swelling of the radial keratotomy incisions. Sometimes subclinical, this postoperative corneal edema may take over 3 months to resolve. Since the effect is transitory, surgeon and patient over-reaction may confound the surgeon-patient relationship if this condition is not recognized. Patients who have had LASIK, PRK, or SMILE may also have hyperopic refractive errors following cataract surgery, but these are not transitory and are often referred to as a refractive "surprise."

pool.q: When performing neodymium yttrium-aluminum-garnet (Nd:YAG) laser posterior capsulotomy, what step is most likely to aid in the prevention of optic pitting?

options.a: increasing the power setting of the laser beam
options.b: posterior defocusing of the laser beam

pool.rationale:
Any posterior chamber intraocular lens (IOL) can be damaged by laser energy, but the threshold for lens damage appears to be lower for silicone than for other materials. The laser pulse should be focused just behind the posterior capsule, although pulses too far behind the IOL will be ineffective at opening the posterior lens capsule. The favored and safest approach is to begin the capsulotomy near the periphery of the intended capsulotomy opening, beginning slightly behind the posterior surface of the capsule and cautiously easing anteriorly until the desired puncture can be achieved at the minimum effective laser energy level, rather than increasing the power settings.
A high-plus-power anterior segment laser lens, used with topical anesthesia, improves ocular stability and enlarges the cone angle of the beam, reducing the depth of focus and decreasing the focus diameter, facilitating laser pulse puncture of the capsule at lower energies, and the structures in front of and behind the lens are less likely to be damaged.
Spiral or circular capsulotomies are less likely to pit the lens centrally, compared to a diamond-shaped capsulotomy, which is typically created by a cruciate pattern intersecting in the center of the axis.
Changing the slit-lamp magnification does nothing to prevent, or cause, IOL optic pitting when performing Nd:YAG capsulotomy.

pool.q: What type of cataract develops specifically as a result of blunt trauma?
pool.rationale: A lens opacity caused by blunt trauma to the eye is classically a stellate or rosette-shaped opacity involving the posterior lens capsule. Anterior polar cataracts are generally bilateral, symmetric, and nonprogressive opacities that are frequently autosomally dominantly inherited. Posterior polar cataracts are sporadic or familial. Iridescent lenticular opacities (Christmas tree) can be seen sporadically, as well as in patients with myotonic dystrophy.

pool.q: Four days after phakic anterior-chamber intraocular lens implantation, a patient develops progressive pain, redness, and blurry vision. In addition, he has anterior chamber inflammation and a hypopyon. What is the best next step in his treatment?

options.a: Control the inflammation by increasing the topical steroid.
options.b: Perform a gonioscopy and treat for uveitis-glaucoma-hyphema (UGH) syndrome.
options.c: Perform a tap and inject procedure with intravitreal antibiotics for presumed endophthalmitis.
options.d: Consider crystalline lens removal, as inflammation can represent capsular violation.

pool.rationale: Any patient with increasing intraocular inflammation with decreased vision and a hypopyon after intraocular surgery should be treated as if the etiology of the inflammation was infectious. Crystalline lens removal would only be indicated if that was the obvious cause of the inflammation. One would be able to observe lens material and a swollen lens. Uveitis-glaucoma-hyphema syndrome would not present this acutely and usually not this early in the postoperative course. Only increasing the steroid without controlling the cause of the inflammation would most likely not be successful.

pool.q: A patient presents after cataract surgery with a shallow anterior chamber and high intraocular pressure. A peripheral iridotomy fails to deepen the chamber or lower the intraocular pressure. What is the next appropriate treatment?

options.a: topical miotics and a second peripheral iridotomy

pool.rationale:
Ciliary block glaucoma (also known as malignant glaucoma, aqueous misdirection, or vitreous block) results from ciliolenticular block induced by anterior movement of the lens–iris diaphragm, poor vitreous fluid conductivity, and choroidal expansion. These factors result in a shallow anterior chamber and secondary elevation of IOP as a consequence of angle obstruction. IOP remains elevated despite the presence of a patent iridectomy or iridotomy.
Medical treatment consists of cycloplegia with atropine and aggressive aqueous suppression with b‑adrenergic antagonists, a‑adrenergic agonists, and/or oral or topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, as well as hyperosmotic agents (such as oral glycerin or intravenous mannitol). Miotics should be avoided because they can make ciliary block glaucoma worse by exacerbating the anterior displacement of the lens–iris diaphragm. Surgical intervention consists of Nd:YAG laser iridozonulohyaloidotomy and, occasionally, vitrectomy to disrupt the anterior vitreous face and vitreous–ciliary body interface.

pool.q: A 68-year-old man has a hypermature cataract in the right eye and has had progressive vision loss over the past 8 months. The posterior pole is not visualized, and the red reflex is absent. He refuses to have cataract surgery. What ocular complication is of greatest risk if cataract surgery is deferred?
pool.rationale: When the entire cortex from the capsule to the nucleus becomes white and opaque, the cataract is said to be mature. In mature opacities, the lens absorbs water, becoming swollen and enlarged (termed intumescent cortical cataract). Such cataracts may lead to angle-closure glaucoma. When degenerated cortical material leaks through the lens capsule, leaving the capsule wrinkled and shrunken, the cataract is referred to as hypermature. The risk of angle closure is reduced in this situation. Although a hypermature cataract does not increase the risk of retinal detachment, the presence of a hypermature cataract can obscure a retinal detachment, or a retinal detachment may be more prone to develop in the presence of chronic poor vision.

pool.q: What carbohydrate metabolism changes occur in the lens in the presence of high levels of glucose?

options.b: Sorbitol is produced and then eliminated from the lens via diffusion through the capsule into the anterior chamber.
options.c: Glucose that is not phosphorylated to G6P enters the Krebs cycle.
options.d: Hexokinase activity increases until all glucose is phosphorylated.

Sorbitol is retained in the lens because of poor permeability, promoting lens opacification.

pool.q: The tunica vasculosa lentis is fully developed at what time of gestation?
pool.rationale: The tunica vasculosa lentis is a capillary network on the posterior surface of the lens capsule that supplies the lens with blood. It arises from the hyaloid artery, which enters the eye at 1 month of gestation. The tunica vasculosa lentis has an anastomosis to the anterior pupillary membrane, which is a capillary network on the anterior surface of the lens. The capillary network surrounding the lens is fully developed around 9 weeks gestation. Before birth, the tunica vasculosa lentis will regress and sometimes leave a small opacity on the posterior lens called a Mittendorf dot. Similarly, the anterior pupillary membrane regresses before birth and can sometimes leave remnants called pupillary strands.

pool.q: Vitreous incarceration in the incision following a cataract operation can cause what complication?

Vitreous in the anterior chamber can lead to chronic intraocular inflammation with or without associated cystoid macular edema (CME). pool.q: What inherited condition typically results in inferonasal subluxation of the lens?

pool.q: What technology is appropriate for evaluating glare disability?

pool.q: An ophthalmologist examines a young patient who has bilateral 20/20 visual acuity and bilaterally symmetric media opacities (one is shown in the figure) that have been present, and stable, since birth. What type of cataract does this patient most likely have?

pool.q: What presumption is the Helmholtz theory of accommodation based on?

options.a: Most of the change in lens shape occurs at the central anterior lens surface.
options.b: As the ciliary muscle contracts, the zonular tension increases, resulting in bulging of the lens and increasing the dioptric power of the eye.
options.c: The change in curvature of the posterior lens capsule contributes about 25% of the accommodative amplitude.
options.d: The action of the anterior zonular fibers on the lens during accommodation results in flattening of the central anterior lens surface.

pool.rationale: The Helmholtz theory of accommodation, developed in the mid-1800s, remains widely accepted. It is based on the presumption that, when a distance target is viewed, the eye's ciliary muscle is relaxed, causing the zonular fibers to flatten the central anterior surface of the lens. Conversely, when the eye attempts to focus on a near object, the ciliary muscle contracts, relaxing the tension on the zonular fibers. The central anterior surface of the lens is allowed to bulge, resulting in an increase in dioptric power. Despite the fact that the central posterior capsule is the thinnest part of the capsule, there is no change in curvature of the posterior aspect of the lens with contraction or relaxation of the ciliary muscle.

pool.q: During a prolonged and complicated cataract surgery requiring an anterior vitrectomy, a patient experiences pain under topical anesthesia. What would be the safest and most effective choice for supplemental anesthesia to complete the procedure?

pool.q: On the first postoperative day after phacoemulsification and posterior chamber IOL implantation, a 67-year-old man presents with mild pain, photophobia, and diffuse corneal edema as shown. The entire central and peripheral cornea are equally affected. There is a marked anterior chamber reaction, but no vitreous inflammation is observed. The cornea in the non-operative eye is normal. What is the most likely cause of his edema?

options.c: response to intraocular solutions used intraoperatively

pool.rationale:
Corneal edema may occur in the immediate postoperative period for a number of reasons, but in this case the diffuse decompensation is most likely, due to toxic anterior segment syndrome (TASS). Onset of corneal edema is higher in eyes with preexisting corneal dysfunction such as Fuchs dystrophy, but this patient has no evidence of having this bilateral disorder, because the other eye is described as normal. Edema may be caused by a combination of mechanical trauma, prolonged surgery, inflammation, and elevated IOP, resulting in acute endothelial decompensation with an increase in corneal thickness, but a combination option is not provided. Toxic substances inadvertently introduced into the anterior chamber can also cause acute endothelial dysfunction, and may produce severe intraocular inflammation, as evidenced by the patient's marked anterior chamber reaction.
The symptoms and signs of TASS may mimic those of infectious endophthalmitis, but are distinguished by diffuse limbus-to-limbus corneal edema, presentation within hours of surgery rather than 2-7 days after surgery was seen in acute infectious endophthalmitis, and lack of vitreous inflammation. A Descemet detachment would be visible and would cause a focal area of stromal swelling and epithelial bullae in the area of detachment.

pool.q: What is the primary treatment modality in managing corneal melting after cataract surgery?

options.a: intensive treatment with topical nonpreserved lubricants

pool.rationale:
Keratolysis, or sterile melting of the cornea, can occur following cataract extraction. It is most frequently associated with autoimmune tear insufficiency syndromes such as keratoconjunctivitis sicca and Sjögren syndrome, systemic autoimmune disease syndromes such as rheumatoid arthritis, and postoperative use of topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), which can also have associations with immune activity in response to toxicity of medicines and preservatives, and cornea hypoesthesia, as do the chronic diseases listed above.
The mainstay of therapy is intensive topical treatment with nonpreserved topical lubricants, withdrawal of topical NSAIDs, and minimizing topical preservative exposure. Additional treatment modalities to encourage epithelialization and to arrest stromal melting include punctal occlusion, bandage contact lenses, tarsorrhaphy, botulinum injections to induce ptosis, and autologous serum eyedrops. In persistent cases, amniotic membrane graft or lamellar or penetrating keratoplasty should be considered.
For the treatment of underlying autoimmune disease, systemic immunosuppressive therapy may be needed. Oral tetracyclines are occasionally given for modulation of meibomian gland activity through their inhibition of matrix metalloproteinases, not specifically for antibiotic effect.

pool.q: Six months ago, a 52-year-old woman underwent surgical repair for a full-thickness macular hole. Now her acuity has fallen to 20/200, and her refractive error has changed from -1.00 to -5.00. What is the most likely cause?

Eyes do not elongate unless a scleral buckle is performed. Posterior staphylomas are unrelated to surgery, but may occur, and patients with them are at increased risk of macular hole. pool.q: What lens capsule finding should a surgeon be prepared for when operating on a patient with aniridia?

Corneal haze and neovascularization in these eyes are common because of stem cell deficiency; capsular staining may aid visualization through the cornea during creation of an adequately sized capsular opening. Use of a high-viscosity OVD also optimizes visualization while stabilizing the capsular surface. The surgeon should avoid working inside the capsular bag to eliminate potential tension on the capsular rim. Low infusion helps reduce turbulence and capsular fluctuation. The capsule in aniridic eyes acts as a pseudo-iris when it opacifies.

pool.q: What creates a vacuum in a phaco machine with a peristaltic pump?

options.a: A vacuum is created as a diaphragm moves in and out.
options.b: A vacuum is created as fluid moves through tubing, causing a relative vacuum at the aspiration port of the phaco tip.
options.c: A vacuum is created by a flow of gas or fluid across a port, proportional to the rate of flow of the gas.
options.d: A vacuum is created in the chamber that closes the exit valve.

Vacuum is flow based and does not build up until the tip is occluded. In a Venturi pump, the vacuum is created proportional to the flow of gas across a port and thus is not flow based, so it can be separately adjusted from aspiration. Similarly, vacuum in a diaphragmatic pump is based on the position of the diaphragm (opening and closing of the exit valve) and thus reaches a preset level independent of aspiration.

pool.q: At what time of gestation do primary lens fibers develop?
pool.rationale:
The embryology of the lens begins with the formation of the optic vesicle at 25 days of gestation from the forebrain. As the optic vesicles enlarge, they come in close contact to the surface ectoderm. Two days later, the surface ectoderm cells over the optic vesicle begin to enlarge and form the lens placode, which then invaginates at 29 days to form the lens pit. The lens pit deepens and forms the lens vesicle. The lens vesicle separates the lens cells from overlying surface ectoderm.
The cells in the posterior layer of the lens vesicle stop dividing and begin to elongate at around 35 days of gestation and are called the primary lens fibers. The primary lens fibers end up being the central portion of the adult lens. The primary lens fibers obliterate the lens vesicle around day 40. Then at week 7, the lens epithelial cells near the equator elongate to form the secondary lens fibers, which form the erect Y-suture anteriorly and inverted Y-suture posteriorly. The Y-sutures are recognizable at 8 weeks.

pool.q: A 76-year-old woman presents with a red, painful eye and an elevated intraocular pressure. She is noted to have corneal edema, a shallow anterior chamber, and a markedly swollen cataract. What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.a: Start topical corticosteroids and aqueous suppressants and examine the patient again in 1-2 months.
options.b: Perform a laser peripheral iridotomy and schedule urgent cataract extraction surgery.
options.c: Perform a laser peripheral iridotomy followed by laser iridoplasty
options.d: Start topical and oral aqueous suppressants and examine the patient again in 3-4 months.

pool.rationale:
This patient has phacomorphic glaucoma. Phacomorphic glaucoma is a form of closed-angle glaucoma caused by a thickened or markedly swollen cataract. The enlarged lens physically pushes the iris forward, which can occlude the angle or can cause glaucoma by a pupillary block mechanism. Treatment begins with topical and/or oral medications to lower pressure. A laser peripheral iridotomy can relieve the pupillary block, but it is not a long-term therapy. Definitive treatment is cataract extraction.
Lens particle glaucoma occurs after the lens capsule is penetrated, either by trauma or by surgery, leading to leakage of lens material in the anterior chamber, which can then clog the trabecular meshwork. This is an example of an open-angle glaucoma. In general, glaucoma follows days to weeks after the inciting event. Steroids and pressure-lowering medications are first-line medical treatment. If the pressure and inflammation cannot be controlled, cataract extraction or further surgery is indicated.
Phacolytic glaucoma results from accumulation of denatured lens proteins that leak through an intact lens capsule. This may occur in mature and hypermature cataracts. Macrophages ingest the lens protein and can clog the trabecular meshwork, leading to glaucoma. Patients typically experience symptoms consistent with acute onset of markedly elevated eye pressure. The anterior chamber is cloudy in appearance and the angle is open. Cataract extraction is the definitive treatment for this condition.
Phacoantigenic (formerly called phacoanaphylactic) glaucoma is a rare entity that can occur after the lens capsule is penetrated, either by trauma or by surgery. It is a granulomatous inflammation with an anterior chamber reaction, including keratic precipitates on the corneal endothelium and/or anterior lens. Topical corticosteroids and aqueous suppressants are used to control this condition. If the pressure and inflammation cannot be controlled, cataract extraction or further surgery is indicated.

pool.q: When performing cataract surgery on a patient who is on anticoagulant therapy (warfarin) and who has a high risk of thromboembolism, what is a correct strategy to reduce the intraoperative risk of bleeding?

options.a: delaying the warfarin dose for 5 days prior to cataract surgery
options.b: use of topical anesthesia instead of a periorbital or retrobulbar block
options.c: administration of intravenous platelet transfusion immediately prior to the operative procedure
options.d: administration of systemic vitamin K immediately prior to the operative procedure

pool.rationale:
A large prospective cohort study did not show an increased risk of hemorrhagic complications in patients on anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy during cataract surgery. In these patients, there is a three-fold increased risk of retrobulbar hemorrhage with retrobulbar injection. Patients undergoing cataract surgery with topical or sub-Tenon anesthesia do not require cessation of anticoagulant therapy.
Administration of vitamin K or platelet transfusion can cause more risk of systemic complications in a patient who has a risk of thromboembolism.
In patients receiving anticoagulation therapy, clear corneal cataract surgery performed with topical anesthesia is not associated with an increased risk of vision-threatening hemorrhagic complications. Minor bleeding problems, such as eyelid ecchymosis, hyphema, and subconjunctival hemorrhage, are more common with anticoagulant use, but these are transient and self-limited. If a retrobulbar block is used, the risk of retrobulbar hemorrhage is higher in patients on anticoagulants. It is important to weigh the systemic risks of discontinuing anticoagulation or antiplatelet therapy with the surgical risks of continuing therapy. When warfarin is continued, the international normalized ratio (INR) is typically maintained within the therapeutic range.
If anticoagulation therapy is to be discontinued or adjusted for surgery, coordination with the prescribing physician is recommended. Discontinuation of anticoagulants is recommended in patients who have previously experienced a suprachoroidal hemorrhage because these patients are predisposed to recurrent bleeding. Time to restoration of normal coagulation is variable and depends on the specific anticoagulant in use; warfarin usually requires 3–5 days. Platelet function resumes 10–21 days after stopping antiplatelet therapy. Typically, it is recommended that patients restart anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy within the first postoperative day. It is important to ask the patient about the use of all medications, including nonprescription items that may contain aspirin, vitamin E, or vitamin K, which could affect coagulation status. Table 12-1 presents a list of anticoagulant and antiplatelet agents approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA).

pool.q: Preoperative administration of mannitol to dehydrate the vitreous body prior to cataract surgery is recommended in what clinical scenario?

In nanophthalmos, there is also an increased risk for uveal effusion. Preoperative administration of IV mannitol to dehydrate the vitreous body, or in some cases, aspiration of liquid vitreous, can help minimize these risks by shrinking vitreous volume and deepening the anterior chamber. Other useful measures in performing cataract surgery on these smaller eyes include using a high-viscosity ophthalmic viscoelastic device (OVD) to protect the corneal endothelium, as well as using a lower aspiration rate or higher infusion pressure during phacoemulsification.
Poor pupillary dilation, pseudoexfoliation, and high myopia are not indications for preoperative mannitol infusion prior to cataract surgery.

The posterior capsule develops a visually significant opacification within the third postoperative week. What is most likely to cause the posterior capsule to opacify so quickly?

options.d: prolonged use of postoperative topical corticosteroids

pool.rationale: The rate of posterior capsule opacification (PCO) appears to be influenced by factors such as history of intraocular inflammation, age of patient, size of capsulorrhexis, quality of cortical cleanup, and time elapsed since surgery. Prolonged use of topical corticosteroids does not appear to influence PCO rates. Silicone appears to have the lowest rate of PCO, and square-edge optic design also has a lower rate of PCO.

pool.q: What is the hallmark of a morgagnian cataract?

options.c: iridescent sheen in the posterior cortical layers

pool.rationale: In a morgagnian cataract, the cortex has liquefied, allowing free movement of the nucleus within the capsular bag. Vacuoles are a characteristic of cortical cataracts. Lenticular myopia is characteristic of nuclear sclerosis. A posterior subcapsular cataract will have an iridescent sheen in the posterior cortical layers.

pool.q: What kind of patient would benefit from Trendelenburg positioning for cataract surgery?

options.a: patient with kyphosis of the spine
options.d: patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease

pool.rationale:
A patient with kyphosis of the spine would benefit from Trendelenburg positioning (placement of the patient in a chair that is then tipped backward so the feet are above the head), which situates the operative eye where it can be more easily accessed by the surgeon.
Patients with obesity, congestive heart failure, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease all benefit from the reduced venous congestion to the head and neck resulting from reverse Trendelenburg positioning.

pool.q: While performing phacoemulsification on a former boxer, the surgeon elects to change the phaco settings. What change would most effectively reduce chances of complications?
pool.rationale: Ocular trauma may result in zonular incompetence. Zonular incompetence becomes apparent intraoperatively with phacodonesis, decentration of the capsular bag, and sometimes vitreous prolapse into the anterior chamber. Phacoemulsification could proceed safely with the same measures used for advanced cataracts. Reducing the flow rate diminishes fluctuation and turbulence in the anterior chamber depth and reduces the risk of vitreous prolapse. The other changes, such as bottle height, phaco power, and vacuum setting, are not as directly related to this situation as aspiration flow rate.

pool.q: What is the most accepted treatment for sustained elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) secondary to retained nuclear material in the anterior chamber?

options.a: breaking the retained nuclear material into small pieces with the yttrium aluminum garnet (YAG) laser for easier absorption
options.c: no treatment, because the condition is usually self-limiting
options.d: surgical removal of the retained nuclear material

pool.rationale:
Retained lens fragments occur in 0.45% to 1.70% of cases after phacoemulsification. Findings may include persistent anterior uveitis, focal corneal edema, and sustained elevated intraocular pressure. Observation is warranted for patients with small amounts of retained cortical lens material in the hope that this material will be reabsorbed.
Nuclear material, even in small amounts, persists longer and is more likely to incite a significant inflammatory reaction and elevated IOP, for which surgical intervention becomes preferred.
Breaking retained nuclear material into smaller fragments with the YAG laser has not been shown to significantly accelerate reabsorption, and may increase inflammation by retaining the same volume but expanding the surface area of the nuclear particles.
Argon laser trabeculoplasty should be avoided in inflammatory glaucomas.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Lens & Cataract — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What refractive surface of the lens undergoes little to no change in curvature with during accommodation at any age?
pool.rationale:
Accommodation is the ability of the eye to focus at near. This is accomplished by contraction of the ciliary muscle, which results in a smaller diameter of the muscle ring, relaxing the tension on the zonular fibers and allowing the lens to take on a more spherical shape. Most of the accommodative change in lens shape occurs at the central anterior lens surface. The central anterior lens capsule is thinner than the peripheral lens capsule, and anterior zonules attach closer to the visual axis than posterior zonular fibers, resulting in a central anterior bulge during accommodation.
The posterior lens curvature changes only minimally during accommodation, and the central posterior lens capsule maintains the same curvature regardless of zonular tension. During accommodation, the axial thickness of the lens increases. Adolescents have 12-16 D of accommodation, adults have 4-8 D, and patients older than 50 years have 2-4 D. The loss of accommodation over time is believed to be due to lens hardening known as presbyopia.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Lens & Cataract — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Following laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) for myopia, if intraocular lens (IOL) power calculations are carried out in a routine manner, what type of refractive error will most likely occur?
pool.rationale:
If standard keratometry readings are used to calculate IOL power for a previously myopic, postkeratorefractive surgery eye, the postoperative refractive error will typically be hyperopic. This is because the keratometry readings are erroneously steeper than the true corneal power, as typically measured several millimeters away from the center of the cornea, and overestimate the flattened curvature of the central optical zone.
Although a variety of methods have been developed to better estimate the central corneal power, and numerous formulas have been developed to calculate IOL powers for postkeratorefractive eyes, variance can still be high, resulting in refractive outcome surprises. As many keratometric methods and IOL calculating formulae as possible should be compared, which can be accomplished simultaneously using the American Society of Cataract and Refractive Surgery (ASCRS) Online Post-Refractive IOL Power Calculator, or other simultaneously calculating tools.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Lens & Cataract — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What serious complication of retrobulbar block is less likely with a peribulbar block?
pool.rationale:
Retrobulbar anesthesia provides excellent ocular akinesia and anesthesia. Complications are uncommon but include retrobulbar hemorrhage; globe penetration; optic nerve trauma; extraocular muscle toxicity; inadvertent intravenous injection associated with cardiac arrhythmias; and inadvertent intradural injection with associated seizures, respiratory arrest, and brainstem anesthesia.
Peribulbar anesthesia theoretically eliminates the risk of complications, such as optic nerve injury and central nervous system (CNS) spread from intradural injection. Globe penetration remains a risk with peribulbar anesthesia and the volume of anesthesia is the same, but into a different location. Postoperative diplopia is similar between the two.

pool.q: While completing a preoperative evaluation for cataract surgery, the ophthalmologist notes that a patient took a systemic alpha-1 adrenergic antagonist for a brief time 10 years ago and is no longer on the medication. What is a potential intraoperative finding based on this information?

options.a: fluctuation of pupil size, with or without poor pupil dilation preoperatively
options.c: shallowing of anterior chamber during phacoemulsification

pool.rationale: Intraoperative floppy iris syndrome (IFIS) can occur after use of systemic alpha-1 adrenergic antagonists, which are commonly prescribed for conditions such as benign prostatic hyperplasia, urinary incontinence, urolithiasis, and hypertension. Even if only one dose is received, years prior to the surgery, the effects may persist indefinitely. Alpha-1 blockers can bind to postsynaptic nerve endings of the iris dilator muscle for prolonged periods, causing excessive iris mobility and the clinical findings of IFIS (poor dilation, fluctuations in pupil size intraoperatively). There is no known risk of anterior chamber shallowing directly because of IFIS, nor of increased risk of suprachoroidal hemorrhage. Systemic hypotension would not be expected with remote use of an alpha-1 receptor antagonist.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Lens & Cataract — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: During routine phacoemulsification of a 3+ posterior subcapsular cataract (PSC), a posterior capsular tear is seen after the removal of the cortex through irrigation and aspiration, and a vitrectomy is necessary. It is determined that an “in-the-bag” IOL placement would not be in order. Generally, what should the power of a sulcus-fixated IOL be?

options.b: the same as that calculated for in-the-bag fixation
options.c: 0.5 to 1.0 D less than that calculated for in-the-bag fixation
options.d: 0.5 to 1.0 D more than that calculated for in-the-bag fixation

pool.rationale: Formulae used for calculating the appropriate IOL power are based on the axial length of the globe, the refracting power of the cornea, and the anticipated postoperative distance between the anterior surface of the cornea and the anterior surface of the IOL (effective, or estimated, lens position, previously referred to as anterior chamber depth). A 3-piece IOL with haptics placed in the ciliary sulcus will have a final lens optic position anterior to the expected optic position of the same IOL in the intracapsular position. Thus, the calculated power of the sulcus-fixated IOL would be expected to be lower than for the intracapsular IOL, typically by 0.50 to 1.00 diopters, which will vary in proportion to the overall dioptric power of the optic, on a continuous gradient.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Lens & Cataract — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the genetic inheritance pattern of galactosemia?
pool.rationale: Galactosemia is a genetic condition caused by an inborn error in galactose metabolism (classically galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase) that can lead to cataracts if left untreated. It is inherited as an autosomal recessive trait. It is not typically autosomal dominant or x-linked.

pool.q: During cataract surgery, a detachment of Descemet membrane usually results from what error?

options.a: using diamond blades for the incision
options.c: catching Descemet membrane with an instrument or intraocular lens (IOL) at the incision site
options.d: having the bottle height too low during cataract surgery

pool.rationale: Detachment of Descemet membrane at the time of cataract surgery occurs when an instrument or IOL is inserted traumatically or when fluid is injected inadvertently into the interface between Descemet membrane and the corneal stroma. Excessive phacoemulsification energy, bottle height, and type of blade are not contributing factors.

pool.q: What is the best indication for the use of a standard capsular tension ring during cataract surgery?

options.a: support of the zonule in the setting of anterior capsular tear
options.b: support of the zonule in the setting of focal absence or weakness of the zonule
options.c: support of the zonule in the setting of lens subluxation
options.d: support of the zonule in the setting of posterior capsular rupture

pool.rationale: Common indications for using a capsular tension ring (CTR) are cases in which zonular support is compromised or in question. Use of a CTR is contraindicated in cases of an anterior or posterior capsular tear. Standard CTRs are most helpful in the setting of focal zonular weakness and perhaps mild global zonular laxity. Support of the zonule in the setting of lens subluxation would probably require a modified (sutured) CTR.

pool.q: Given the schematic below, what are the thicknesses associated with each part of the lens capsule indicated by the letters A, B, C, D, and E?

options.a: A: 14 µm, B: 4 µm, C: 17 µm, D: 23 µm, E: 21 µm
options.b: A: 14 µm, B: 21 µm, C: 17 µm, D: 4 µm, E: 4 µm
options.c: A: 14 µm, B: 21 µm, C: 17 µm, D: 23 µm, E: 4µm
options.d: A: 4 µm, B: 14 µm, C: 4 µm, D: 17 µm, E: 4 µm

pool.rationale: These relative thicknesses just have to be memorized. The thinnest area of the capsule is the central posterior pole. It is thickest in the anterior and posterior preequatorial zones (B and D). The anterior capsule increases throughout life. Of note, the lens capsule is an elastic, transparent basement membrane that is made up of type IV collagen.

pool.q: In the case of high axial myopia, what condition might cause an unexpected large postoperative refractive error?

options.a: prior retinal detachment with scleral buckle

pool.rationale: A posterior staphyloma is usually associated with high myopia. If the axial length is measured from the cornea to the posterior staphyloma, the length will be falsely longer, resulting in an intraocular lens power that is too low. The depth of the anterior chamber, flat keratometry readings, or the presence of a scleral buckle would not make the determination of axial length more challenging.

pool.q: What is the inheritance pattern of the condition commonly associated with this type of cataract?
pool.rationale: The figure shows a "Christmas tree" cataract. This type of cataract is most commonly associated with myotonic dystrophy. These polychromatic iridescent crystals are found in the lens cortex and composed of plasmalemma from the lens fibers. These crystals can also be observed in patients without myotonic dystrophy and are thought to be caused by cholesterol crystal deposition. Myotonic dystrophy is an autosomal dominant condition characterized by delayed muscle relaxation, generalized muscle weakness, frontal balding in male patients, and cardiac conduction defects. Other ocular manifestations include ptosis, orbicularis oculi weakness, progressive external ophthalmoplegia, exotropia, and poor Bell phenomenon.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Lens & Cataract — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: During the evaluation of a man with a left brow laceration, the ophthalmologist notices a hook-shaped copper wire in the left anterior chamber that penetrates the anterior capsule. A small, stellate, refractile lens opacity is eccentric to the visual axis. The eye is otherwise uninflamed, with visual acuity of 20/30 and normal intraocular pressure. The patient has no recollection of injury to or pain in eye. What would be the preferred management?

options.a: performing an anterior chamber tap for culture
options.b: surgically removing the intraocular foreign body
options.c: watchful waiting unless an opacity forms, affecting vision, or the eye becomes inflamed

pool.rationale:
Chalcosis occurs when an copper-containing intraocular foreign body (IOFB) corrodes and leaves deposits in the Descemet membrane, anterior lens capsule, or other intraocular basement membranes. Given the presence of a copper-containing IOFB that penetrates the anterior capsule, the development of lens-related inflammation and later chalcosis is nearly assured if the lens and IOFB are not promptly removed.
Copper rarely leads to retinal degeneration or reduced electroretinogram amplitudes, as is common with iron-containing IOFBs, which cause siderosis. An anterior chamber tap is not indicated, as there is no evidence of endophthalmitis or acute intraocular infection.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Lens & Cataract — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Which types of intraocular lenses (IOLs) have been associated with the highest rates of corneal decompensation?
pool.rationale: Among the IOL designs that have been associated with corneal endothelial cell loss are iris-clip lenses and closed-loop ACIOLs. Chronic inflammation and contact between the lens and peripheral corneal endothelial cells are thought to be causes of this loss. Development of the flexible-loop ACIOL and advances in the open support arms with 4-point fixation have allowed the ACIOL to remain a treatment choice for cases with compromised capsular support.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Lens & Cataract — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: An ophthalmologist is performing femtosecond laser-assisted cataract surgery on a patient with a dense nucleus. After laser creation of the corneal incisions, capsulorhexis, and lens fragmentation, the surgeon moves the patient from the femtosecond laser to the operating microscope for phacoemulsification. As the surgeon begins hydrodissection, the lens nucleus immediately falls into the vitreous cavity. What is the most likely reason this complication occurred?

options.a: The dense cataract led to an error in laser depth estimation, and the laser hit the posterior capsule during lens fragmentation, causing a posterior capsule rupture that enlarged during hydrodissection.
options.b: The trauma of the femtosecond laser docking procedure led to zonular damage, causing the lens to dislocate as soon as it was manipulated during hydrodissection.
options.c: Microscopic movement of the lens nucleus during lens fragmentation weakened the posterior capsule, leading to rupture during hydrodissection.
options.d: Gas bubble formation in the capsular bag and the resulting increase in pressure within the bag caused a posterior capsule rupture during hydrodissection.

pool.rationale:
The femtosecond laser is known to cause gas bubble formation within the lens and capsular bag. During aggressive hydrodissection, the pressure can increase within the bag and cause a posterior capsule rupture, resulting in the nucleus dropping into the vitreous cavity.
Another complication of femtosecond laser-assisted cataract surgery is incomplete capsulorhexis formation. This could lead to a radial tear of the anterior capsule, which could wrap around and cause a posterior capsule tear.
The femtosecond laser uses OCT technology to determine the depth of laser treatment and would not be expected to directly damage the posterior capsule. Any microscopic movement of the lens during fragmentation would not be expected to damage the posterior capsule. The docking procedure commonly causes subconjunctival hemorrhage, but should not damage zonules.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Lens & Cataract — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What criterion determines the type of intervention that should be performed for post-cataract extraction endophthalmitis, based on the Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study?

options.b: degree of inflammation in the vitreous
options.c: amount of time that has passed since surgery

pool.rationale: As a result of the EVS study, immediate pars plana vitrectomy and antibiotic injections are recommended when the patient's visual acuity is light perception. When the vision is hand motions or better, a less-invasive anterior chamber and vitreous biopsy for cultures, with subsequent intravitreal injection of antibiotics, may be sufficient. Intravitreal corticosteroids are frequently used although not proven to be beneficial in a controlled study. Intravenous or oral antibiotics were not shown to be of much benefit.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Lens & Cataract — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What type of cataract is characteristic of ischemic ocular conditions?
pool.rationale: Ocular ischemic conditions such as Takayasu arteritis,  Buerger disease, and anterior segment necrosis characteristically result in posterior subcapsular cataract, which can progress to complete opacification of the entire lens.

pool.q: Over the long term, what astigmatic shift is expected to occur with limbal incisions for extracapsular cataract extraction (ECCE)?

options.a: steepening of the axis oriented toward the incision when done in hyperopes but a flattening in myopes
options.b: flattening of the axis oriented toward the incision
options.c: steepening of the axis oriented toward the incision
options.d: flattening of the axis oriented toward the incision when done in myopes but a steepening in hyperopes

pool.rationale: Initially, tight sutures may cause the corneal curvature to steepen in the axis of the incision. However, with time, the sutures will relax or even dissolve, causing flattening in the axis of the incision. This scenario does not depend on whether the patient is hyperopic or myopic.

pool.q: When performing Nd:YAG laser capsulotomy on a patient with a plate-haptic silicone intraocular lens (IOL), the risk of lens dislocation can be reduced by placing laser applications in what pattern?
pool.rationale: For plate-haptic IOLs, the tension force exerted on the peripheral capsule can lead to radial extension of any capsular opening. For this reason, a spiraling circular pattern of Nd:YAG spots is recommended to reduce radialization and lower the risk of plate-haptic IOL dislocation. Patterns that require initial Nd:YAG spot placement near the pupillary margin or that result in radial tearing (such as a cruciate pattern) are less desirable in this setting.

pool.q: If a ground-glass appearance of the cornea is noted immediately after surgery, what condition should the surgeon suspect?

options.b: entrance of a toxic substance into the eye intraoperatively

pool.rationale: The timing is a key difference between this and the other causes of corneal edema. A chemical insult to the cornea such as preservatives or improper concentration of solutions can cause a rapid onset corneal edema. Acute infectious endophthalmitis typically develops 2 to 7 days after surgery. Fuchs corneal dystrophy generally will not cause an immediate corneal edema. Mechanical trauma will generally cause a localized edema at the site of the trauma.

pool.q: What agent, when placed in the conjunctival fornix prior to surgery, has been associated with a decrease in culture-proven endophthalmitis?

options.c: antibacterial soap prior to 10% solution of povidone-iodine

pool.rationale: A 5% solution of povidone-iodine, not scrub or soap, placed in the conjunctival fornix has been shown to decrease bacterial counts and postoperative endophthalmitis.

pool.q: As a newborn, a patient had seizures, vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice, and bilateral congenital cataracts, one of which is shown. Early diagnosis and therapy cleared the cataracts without surgery. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale: Galactosemia is associated with "oil droplet" type cataracts, as shown in the figure. It is also associated with seizures and jaundice, as described. Hypocalcemia cataracts are punctate iridescent opacities in the anterior and posterior cortex. Alport syndrome is associated with anterior lenticonus. Wilson disease is associated with sunflower cataracts, in which reddish-brown pigment is deposited in the anterior lens capsule and subcapsular cortex in a stellate shape.

pool.q: What is the appropriate management of a Descemet membrane detachment noted intraoperatively during cataract surgery?

options.a: Perform a relaxing incision over the area of the detachment.
options.b: Reposition and tamponade the membrane with air or sulfur hexafluoride (SF6) gas.
options.d: Remove as much of the loose membrane as possible.

pool.rationale:
6) gas.

Inadvertent fluid or instrument dissection between the corneal stroma and Descemet membrane, at either the primary cataract surgery incision or the sideport incision, may result in a small or large detachment of Descemet membrane. Small detachments may resolve spontaneously. Otherwise, they can be reattached with air or expansile gas (eg, sulfur hexafluoride [SF6] or perfluoropropane [C3F8]) tamponade in the anterior chamber. The expansile gas can help position larger detachments prior to placement of sutures, if they are needed. One or more double-armed 10-0 nylon or polypropylene full-thickness mattress sutures pass from the endothelial/Descemet surface and are tied with buried knots on the external epithelial surface.
An ophthalmic viscosurgical device (OVD) can facilitate chamber maintenance during the procedure, but the surgeon must take great care not to introduce the OVD between Descemet membrane and the corneal stroma. Although gas and fluid may occasionally be released through a very small, extra-axial, externally penetrating incision through the corneal stroma, relaxing incisions over the area of Descemet detachment are not a primary approach to management. Descemet membrane tissue should be preserved to the fullest extent possible, not removed.

pool.q: A girl with a history of atopic dermatitis has been maintained on topical corticosteroids, phototherapy, and antihistamines. At age 14, her best corrected vision is 20/100 OU. What is the most likely cause?
pool.rationale: Cataract formation has been reported in 5%-38% of patients with atopic dermatitis. The cataracts are most often bilateral, anterior subcapsular opacities that resemble shieldlike plaques and usually develop in the second or third decades of life. Steroid-induced glaucoma and posterior subcapsular cataract may be associated with topical corticosteroids, but this is less likely. UV corneal burn would be a rare complication of phototherapy if adequate safeguards were undertaken.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Lens & Cataract — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: In what situation is postoperative transient hyperopia after cataract surgery more commonly encountered?

options.b: in eyes with high levels of astigmatism
options.c: in eyes that have undergone photorefractive keratectomy (PRK)
options.d: in eyes that have undergone radial keratotomy (RK)

pool.rationale: The corneal incisions in RK often swell after cataract surgery, causing flattening of the cornea and transient hyperopia. In eyes that have undergone PRK, highly myopic eyes, and eyes with high levels of astigmatism, there are no factors to increase the risk of postoperative hyperopia.

pool.q: During cataract extraction, the ophthalmologist performs a continuous curvilinear capsulorrhexis. After subsequent hydrodissection, the ophthalmologist notices anterior movement of the entire iris-lens diaphragm and collapse of the anterior chamber. The IOP is high, and the patient is not experiencing any significant pain. Placement of viscoelastic gel does not reform the anterior chamber. What is the most likely cause of this phenomenon?
pool.rationale: In rare cases, the fluid infused into the anterior chamber may be misdirected into the vitreous cavity, causing an increase in the vitreous volume, with subsequent forward displacement of the lens and shallowing of the anterior chamber. The fluid may accumulate in the retrolenticular space or dissect posteriorly along the vitreoretinal interface. This complication, called posterior infusion syndrome, is most likely to occur during hydrodissection, when fluid is forcefully injected into the capsular bag. A shallow anterior chamber resulting from posterior infusion syndrome may indicate loss of integrity of the capsular bag. As to the other choices, choroidal hemorrhage is typically painful. An empty infusion bottle would not apply in this situation as the case had not yet proceeded to the phacoemulsification or irrigation/ aspiration. A Valsalva maneuver may cause posterior pressure in the eye but not cause a noticeably high pressure.

pool.q: When a suprachoroidal hemorrhage is suspected during anterior segment surgery, what is the best management option?

options.a: Perform one or more posterior sclerotomies.
options.b: Continue the surgery with close observation for worsening.
options.c: Open the eye anteriorly to lower intraocular pressure.

pool.rationale:
A suprachoroidal hemorrhage is a rare condition that usually occurs intraoperatively, often accompanied by a dramatic increase in intraocular pressure, pain, darkening of the red reflex, incision gape, and prolapse of the iris. This can progress to an expulsive choroidal hemorrhage in which intraocular contents egress from the eye.
Immediate intervention to close the open incision is thus necessary in the setting of suprachoroidal hemorrhage. Opening the eye anteriorly or proceeding with surgery would potentially worsen the hemorrhage. Posterior sclerotomies to expel suprachoroidal blood would be reasonable in some situations, but only after an attempt to seal the wound had been made.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Lens & Cataract — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Aside from axial myopia, what is the biggest risk factor for rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RRD) after cataract surgery?

options.a: the presence of a posterior vitreous detachment in the eye prior to cataract surgery

pool.rationale: Risk factors for RRD include axial myopia (greater than 25 mm), younger age, male sex, lattice degeneration of the retina, previous retinal tear/detachment in the operated eye, history of retinal detachment in the fellow eye, or family history of retinal detachment. Most RRD are sequelae of posterior vitreous detachments.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Lens & Cataract — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What medication might have placed this patient at risk for the intraoperative complication shown in the figure?
pool.rationale: Patients taking alfuzosin develop floppy iris syndrome, a major risk factor for the development of intraoperative iridodialysis. Nonpharmacologic risk factors for iridodialysis include poor wound construction, shallow anterior chamber, multiple entries and exits of instruments through wound, iris prolapse, surgical manipulation of iris, or floppy iris syndrome. Alfuzosin is an α1 adrenergic antagonist, a family of drugs associated with floppy iris syndrome, and is used orally for the treatment of benign prostatic hypertrophy. Epinephrine is sometimes used to provide extra dilation in cases of floppy iris syndrome but is not a cause or risk factor of iridodialysis. Atropine would dilate the pupil and shift the iris diaphragm posteriorly, deepening the anterior chamber, pulling the iris further from a surgical wound. Warfarin use is unrelated to iridodialysis, but could aggravate hyphema if one occurred.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Lens & Cataract — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Adequate preoperative treatment of blepharitis prior to cataract surgery may help to reduce the incidence of what complication?
pool.rationale: Blepharitis should be controlled before surgery in order to reduce the risk of endophthalmitis. Uncontrolled blepharitis causing irritation and an unhealthy tear film may adversely impact the quality of vision after cataract surgery. Blepharitis does not increase the risk of corneal melts, macular edema, or refractive surprise.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Lens & Cataract — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What type of infantile cataract is characterized by a group of club-shaped cortical opacities around the lens equator?
pool.rationale:
Coronary cataracts consist of group of club-shaped cortical opacities arranged like a crown (or corona) around the lens equator.
Cerulean cataracts (also known as blue-dot cataracts) consist of bluish opacities in the cortex. Nuclear cataracts are opacities of the embryonic or both the embryonic and fetal lens nucleus. Capsular cataracts refer to opacifications of the lens epithelium and anterior capsule that spare the lens cortex.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Lens & Cataract — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What symptom is associated specifically with nuclear cataract?

options.b: decreased vision with near more than distance vision

pool.rationale: The hardening of the lens nucleus causes a myopic shift. In hyperopic or emmetropic eyes this shift enables presbyopes to read without correction, a condition referred to as "second sight." Glare from car headlights is typically noted with cortical cataracts and posterior subcapsular cataracts. Monocular diplopia can be present in nuclear, cortical, and posterior subcapsular cataracts. Decreased vision at near more than distance vision is a characteristic of posterior subcapsular cataracts.

pool.q: During the capsulorrhexis portion of cataract surgery, the ophthalmologist notices that the lens nucleus and the capsular bag rotate along with tearing of the anterior capsule. What maneuver would be recommended at this decision point?

options.a: Add more viscoelastic gel and pull the capsular flap more peripherally.
options.b: Regrasp the flap near the tear frequently and complete the capsulorrhexis.
options.c: Insert a second instrument through the paracentesis to push the lens posteriorly and stabilize the nucleus.
options.d: Use capsular hooks to stabilize the bag.

pool.rationale: Movement of the lens and capsule with traction indicates that there is a weak or damaged zonule. Continued traction on the capsular flap could break zonular fibers, which may lead to a dropped nucleus or a capsular rupture. Use of capsular hooks may improve visualization, and a capsular tension ring may stabilize the bag to allow completion of the capsulorrhexis. Adding more ophthalmic viscosurgical gel or pulling the tear more peripherally further strains the remaining zonular fibers. Pressing down on the lens with a second instrument also strains the zonule. Regrasping the flap frequently is often a good idea for controlling the size of the capsulorrhexis, but this method does not protect the zonule from damage, as the same force must be applied to tear the capsule no matter where it is grasped.

pool.q: During phacoemulsification, the surgeon realizes that zonular dialysis of 3 clock-hours (90°) is present. How should the surgeon proceed?

options.a: Place a capsular tension ring (CTR) or capsular hooks, complete phacoemulsification, and insert a posterior-chamber IOL.
options.b: Proceed with phacoemulsification and place an anterior-chamber IOL.
options.c: Increase the bottle height and flow rate to maintain adequate anterior chamber depth.
options.d: Close the corneal incision and convert to an extracapsular cataract extraction with a superior corneoscleral incision.

pool.rationale:
For a patient with 90° of zonular dialysis, management consists of continued phacoemulsification and CTR placement. The timing of the CTR placement depends on the extent of the zonular compromise and the surgeon's preference. Placement of the CTR before completion of phacoemulsification stabilizes the capsule for further lens manipulation and extraction, but makes cortical aspiration more difficult. Thorough cortical aspiration is easier if CTR placement is delayed until just before IOL insertion. However, there is a risk of extending the zonular dialysis if phacoemulsification is performed without adequate capsule support.
The flow rate and bottle height should not be increased, because doing so could cause vitreous to prolapse through the dialysis and into the anterior chamber. OVD can be used as a tamponade against the forward movement of vitreous in the area of the dialysis. Unless the situation deteriorates further, neither conversion to extracapsular cataract extraction nor use of an anterior-chamber IOL would be necessary.

pool.q: What intervention is most appropriate to minimize the risk of intraoperative iris prolapse through the cataract incision?

options.a: cessation of alpha-1a antagonist medication prior to surgery
options.b: discontinuation of fluid inflow prior to withdrawal of instruments
options.c: intracameral injection of local anesthetic such as preservative-free lidocaine
options.d: creation of a wide surgical incision

pool.rationale:
Iris prolapse through the cataract incision is an intraoperative complication that may be more likely in the setting of intraoperative floppy iris syndrome (IFIS). The risk of iris prolapse may be decreased by a variety of interventions, including employment of highly retentive ophthalmic viscosurgical devices (OVDs) to “viscodilate” the pupil and maintain a concave iris near the incisions, discontinuation of fluid inflow prior to withdrawal of instruments to prevent fluid and iris egress, and the use of low-flow settings to minimize anterior chamber turbulence and eliminate a higher pressure gradient posterior to the iris.
Intracameral anesthetic injection does not affect the risk of iris prolapse. Creation of a wide surgical incision would possibly increase the risk of iris prolapse. Although the use of alpha-1a antagonist medications such as tamsulosin is a risk factor for IFIS, there is no evidence that cessation of the medication diminishes the risk for IFIS and therefore the risk for iris prolapse.
Intraoperative iris prolapse through the cataract incision entry site is best managed by replacement of the prolapsed iris after decreasing anterior chamber pressure through the side port incision. Excision of prolapsed iris can be necessary if the iris cannot be repositioned.

pool.q: What is the primary effect of increasing the flow rate of a peristaltic pump phacoemulsification machine?

options.b: increased followability to the phaco tip
options.c: slower buildup of vacuum following occlusion of the phaco tip

pool.rationale: The aspiration system of phaco machines varies according to pump design. The 3 types of pumps are peristaltic, diaphragm, and Venturi. Vacuum response time with the peristaltic type of pump is relatively rapid; linear control is achieved as the speed of the rollers is increased. Vacuum is flow-based and does not build up until the tip is occluded. Increasing the flow rate will increase followability at the phaco tip. Faster buildup of vacuum will occur following occlusion with increased flow rate. The incisional outflow is related to wound construction. Anterior chamber depth can be altered by bottle height.

pool.q: What test should be performed in a patient who has low intraocular pressure (1-3 mm Hg) 6 weeks after uncomplicated cataract surgery, but who has no visible filtering bleb and whose Seidel test result is negative?
pool.rationale:
Inadvertent creation of a cyclodialysis cleft after cataract surgery is a common finding with consistently low intraocular pressure (IOP) in the early to mid-postoperative period. Gonioscopy is indicated to detect the deep-angle recess with a gap between the sclera and the ciliary body.
A B scan ultrasonography and/or UBM would be performed after dilated eye examination to check for suprachoroidal hemorrhage (which presents with elevated IOP) or low anterior choroidals (which present with low IOP). Repeat Seidel testing would be indicated for detection of a wound leak.

pool.q: What enzyme protects the lens from free radical or oxidative damage?
pool.rationale: The lens contains several enzymes that protect against free radical or oxidative damage, including superoxide dismutase, catalase, and glutathione peroxidase. Superoxide dismutase catalyzes the destruction of the superoxide anion, O2– , and produces hydrogen peroxide. Fructokinase, lactic dehydrogenase, and hexokinase are not involved in this protective role.

pool.q: The finding shown in the picture is strongly associated with what factor during cataract surgery?

options.c: use of a one-piece acrylic IOL

pool.rationale: Progressive capsular contraction, or capsular phimosis, is common in eyes with pseudoexfoliation. This patient developed complete phimosis of the anterior capsular opening. Risk factors leading to this phenomenon include a small capsulorrhexis, abnormal zonular support, use of a silicone plate haptic IOL, and retinopathy of prematurity. Capsular opacification stems from the continued viability of lens epithelial cells remaining after removal of the nucleus and cortex. These cells can proliferate in several patterns.

pool.q: An ophthalmologist is planning to perform cataract surgery on a patient with benign essential blepharospasm. What anesthetic block would be most appropriate in this scenario?
pool.rationale:
While not commonly used with modern small-incision cataract surgical techniques, a facial nerve block can help prevent eyelid squeezing intraoperatively. In the case of a patient with benign essential blepharospasm, this technique would be beneficial in blocking contraction of the orbicularis oculi.
Although peribulbar, retrobulbar, and sub-Tenon blocks are valuable ocular anesthetic techniques for cataract surgery, they would not address forcible eyelid closure.

pool.q: A 55-year-old pseudophakic man suddenly develops abrupt visual decline, and among his clinical findings is the image below. What is the most common clinical condition associated with this finding?
pool.rationale: Intracapsular intraocular lens (IOL) dislocation results from zonular degradation. Zonules may be found to be insufficient or become degraded in conjunction with many conditions, including congenital zonulopathies, uveitis and other inflammatory zonulopathies, retinitis pigmentosa, high myopia, prior trauma or surgery, anterior capsule contraction and phimosis after cataract surgery, and bag-placed IOLs. However, the most common cause is zonular degradation associated with pseudoexfoliation syndrome.

pool.q: How is metabolic waste removed from the crystalline lens?

options.a: It is removed via the aqueous humor.
options.b: It is broken down by lysosomes.
options.c: It is stored in the lens, not removed, contributing to the increase in lens size throughout life.
options.d: It is absorbed by the vitreous.

pool.rationale: After fetal development, the lens has no blood supply and the lens fibers have no organelles. Waste removal depends on the aqueous humor. Changes in lens size occur throughout life as the lens epithelial cells at the equator continue to divide.

pool.q: Cataracts induced by ionizing radiation (eg, gamma rays and X-rays) typically occur how long after exposure?
pool.rationale: The lens is extremely sensitive to ionizing radiation; however, as much as 20 years may pass after exposure before a cataract becomes clinically apparent. The period of latency is related to the dose of radiation and to the patient's age; younger patients are more susceptible because they have more actively growing lens cells.

pool.q: When performing cataract surgery on a patient with a posterior polar cataract, what technique should be avoided?
pool.rationale: Hydrodissection carries the risk that the fluid wave could rupture the weakened posterior capsule. Gentle hydrodelineation can be helpful to mobilize the lens. Phaco chop and divide-and-conquer methods of lens removal can be used at the surgeon's discretion.

pool.q: What examination finding separates capsular block syndrome from aqueous misdirection?

options.d: space between intraocular lens (IOL) and posterior capsule

pool.rationale:
Capsular block syndrome is caused by trapped viscoelastic or aqueous fluid behind an IOL in an intact capsular bag, leading to a large space between the IOL and the posterior capsule. The posterior capsular distention pushes the IOL forward, uniformly shallows the anterior chamber, and causes a myopic refractive shift. The anterior chamber narrowing can lead to a rise in intraocular pressure.
Aqueous misdirection also leads to a uniformly shallow anterior chamber with an anteriorly displaced IOL. This condition can also lead to elevated intraocular pressure.
Neither aqueous misdirection nor capsular block syndrome is associated with peripheral choroidal detachment or iris bombé.

pool.q: An ophthalmologist is consulted to see a 19-year-old inpatient who has been admitted for altered mental status, fatigue, nausea, abdominal pain, and splenomegaly. His cornea is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale: Wilson disease (hepatolenticular degeneration) is an inherited autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism. The characteristic ocular manifestation of Wilson disease is the Kayser-Fleischer ring, a golden-brown discoloration of the Descemet membrane around the periphery of the cornea, as shown in the photo. The photo clearly shows the Kayser-Fleischer ring of Wilson disease and is not characteristic of AIDS, Whipple disease, or hepatitis B.

pool.q: What type of cataract classically causes marked glare disability at near while maintaining reasonably good distance Snellen visual acuity?
pool.rationale: Posterior subcapsular cataracts will cause a worsening of vision in any situation where pupillary miosis is present. Nuclear, cortical, and morgagnian cataracts will typically cause more symmetric vision loss.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Lens & Cataract — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the typical cataract type in patients with myotonic dystrophy?
pool.rationale: Patients with myotonic dystrophy typically develop polychromatic iridescent crystals in the lens cortex. Wilson disease is associated with a sunflower cataract. Posterior subcapsular cataracts are very common and can be associated with long-term corticosteroid use. Anterior polar cataracts are usually small and bilateral and do not impair vision. They are frequently inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Lens & Cataract — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: The image below shows an eye with a closed-loop anterior IOL. In this context, the image (Fig. 1) most likely represents what common complication?
pool.rationale: The image shows a closed-loop IOL and diffuse corneal edema consistent with pseudophakic bullous keratopathy. Corneal decompensation is believed to result from peripheral endothelium-lens contact. Anterior chamber intraocular lenses (ACIOLs) are at risk for angle-closure episodes, but the anterior chamber appears formed in the image above. Choroidal detachments are not increased by closed-loop or anterior chamber IOLs. A Descemet membrane detachment would result in localized, not diffuse, corneal edema.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Lens & Cataract — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: During insertion of an aspheric single-piece intraocular lens (IOL) with the standard lens inserter during cataract surgery, the IOL is noted to be twisted into an "S" shape. What potential complication is associated with this intraoperative finding?

options.b: loss of asphericity and refractive surprise

pool.rationale: Incorrect insertion of an aspheric single-piece IOL will result in a refractive surprise. In a non–wavefront-optimized IOL, it will be a small myopic shift. The optical result of backwards insertion of a wavefront-optimized IOL is not as predictable. Placement of an angulated IOL upside down can cause the IOL to vault anteriorly so that it becomes captured by iris, leading to pupillary-block glaucoma. UGH syndrome can exist if there is contact between the lens haptics and uveal tissue when the haptics are misplaced in the sulcus. Pigment dispersion and pigmentary glaucoma can occur when there is IOL sulcus placement with iris-optic or iris-haptic contact.

pool.q: A 68-year-old man from Nigeria requests cataract surgery for his left eye. His right eye has a central corneal scar from a dart injury at age 6. His best corrected vision is 20/400 OD and 20/30 OS. He has moderate nuclear sclerosis in the left eye. What management is recommended for this patient?

options.a: Offer cataract surgery and cover risks of surgery carefully.
options.b: Decline cataract surgery because of the patient's monocularity.
options.c: Ascertain whether his daily activities are affected by his vision.
options.d: Offer penetrating keratoplasty for the right eye.

pool.rationale: Before elective surgery is undertaken, the ophthalmologist must understand how the vision deficit is interfering with the patient's life. Cataract surgery  may be reasonable in this situation, but only if the patient indicates that the decreased vision is a hardship for him.

pool.q: What test is useful in the calculation of intraocular lens (IOL) power for a patient who has previously undergone laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK)?

options.d: optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the macula

pool.rationale: Corneal topography is useful to determine whether there is irregular astigmatism and to determine the true corneal power. Although OCT of the anterior segment might provide useful measurements such as anterior chamber depth and corneal thickness, macular OCT does not assist in the calculation of IOL power. Immersion A-scan ultrasonography can be used in place of optical biometry, but contact A-scan is not accurate enough for IOL calculation in patients who have undergone refractive surgery.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Lens & Cataract — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What type of congenital cataract is depicted in this photo?
pool.rationale: Sutural cataracts are opacifications of the Y-suture of the fetal nucleus. Sutural cataracts are usually bilateral, nonvisually significant, and can be inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion. Coronary cataracts are cortical opacities arranged around the equator of the lens like a corona (crown). Cerulean cataracts (blue-dot cataracts) are bluish opacities within the lens cortex. Lamellar cataracts are opacifications within specific layers or zones of the lens and frequently take on a disc-shaped configuration. Lamellar cataracts are the most common type of congenital cataract.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Lens & Cataract — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What part of the lens are colobomas most commonly located in?
pool.rationale: A lens coloboma is an anomaly of lens shape. Primary coloboma is a wedge-shaped defect or indentation of the lens periphery that occurs as an isolated anomaly. Secondary coloboma is a flattening or indentation of the lens periphery caused by the lack of ciliary body or zonular development. Lens colobomas are typically located inferonasally and can be associated with colobomas of the iris, optic nerve, or retina. Cortical lens opacification or thickening of the lens capsule can appear adjacent to the coloboma. The zonular attachments in the region of the coloboma are usually weakened or absent.

pool.q: Staining of the anterior lens capsule prior to creation of the capsulorrhexis is most useful when what clinical scenario is encountered during phacoemulsification?
pool.rationale: Staining of the anterior lens capsule prior to phacoemulsification is most useful in the setting of a poor red reflex. Capsular staining, typically achieved with Trypan blue, may enhance visualization of the capsulorrhexis edge in the setting of dense cortical opacification, brunescent nuclear sclerosis, and other cataracts where an abnormal red reflex impedes this discrimination.

pool.q: Manual extracapsular cataract surgery may be preferred over phacoemulsification in what situation?

options.a: in eyes where postoperative inflammation is to be minimized
options.b: in patients with extremely dense nuclei
options.c: in patients with previous glaucoma filtering blebs
options.d: in patients who desire rapid visual recovery postoperatively

pool.rationale: Manual extracapsular cataract surgery may be the preferred technique in the setting of an extremely dense cataract. Surgery in the setting of a previous filtering surgery will be best performed with minimal manipulation of the conjunctiva, so clear corneal phacoemulsification would be preferred. In most situations, phacoemulsification will result in a more rapid recovery of vision and reduced inflammation when compared to other techniques.

pool.q: An 80-year-old patient who underwent cataract extraction with intraocular lens (IOL) implantation 8 weeks ago presents today with decreased vision from 20/20 postoperatively to 20/40, and the finding shows in the figure below. If the patient has a history of corticosteroid-responsive glaucoma, prior herpes simplex keratitis, and a sulfa allergy, what would be the best management?
pool.rationale: Given this patient's history, findings, and course, he has characteristic features of pseudophakic cystoid macular edema (p-CME). Medical therapeutic options for CME include topical corticosteroid and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) drops, posterior sub-Tenon corticosteroid injection, oral NSAIDs, oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, and intravitreal corticosteroid injection. However, given that the patient has steroid-responsive glaucoma and corneal herpetic disease, steroids in any form would be a poor initial choice. Herpes keratitis can be reactivated with the use of topical steroids. Oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitors are relatively contraindicated for patients allergic to sulfa drugs.

pool.q: A 34-year-old Asian female is diagnosed with Takayasu arteritis and is told that she is at risk of developing early-onset cataracts. What type of cataract is this patient at risk of developing secondary to her medical condition?

options.a: Patients with Takayasu arteritis are predisposed to formation of anterior subcapsular cataracts.
options.b: Patients with Takayasu arteritis are not predisposed to cataract formation.
options.c: Patients with Takayasu arteritis are predisposed to formation of nuclear sclerotic cataracts.
options.d: Patients with Takayasu arteritis are predisposed to formation of posterior subcapsular cataracts.

pool.rationale: Takayasu arteritis, also known as "pulseless disease" or "aortic arch disease," is a large-vessel vasculitis that is common in young to middle-aged women of Asian descent. It can lead to ocular ischemia. Ischemic conditions can predispose to the formation of posterior subcapsular cataracts (PSC). Other forms of ischemia-related conditions include thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease) and anterior segment necrosis. These cataracts can progress rapidly to complete opacification.
