pool.q: Compared to large-incision extracapsular cataract extraction (ECCE), what postoperative complication is more common when performing intracapsular cataract extraction (ICCE)?
pool.rationale: Due to the loss of the barrier between the anterior and posterior segments, the risk of retinal detachment is higher with ICCE than with ECCE or phacoemulsification. Anterior chamber lens dislocation, induced astigmatism, and endophthalmitis rates are similar with large-incision ECCE and ICCE.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Lens & Cataract — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What congenital disorder is microspherophakia associated with?
pool.rationale: Microspherophakia is a developmental abnormality in which the lens is small in diameter and spherical. It is most often associated with Weill-Marchesani syndrome, but can also be associated with Peters anomaly, Marfan syndrome, Alport syndrome, Lowe syndrome, and congenital rubella.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Lens & Cataract — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is an indication for combined keratoplasty and cataract extraction?

options.a: brunescent cataract and cornea guttata with normal corneal thickness
options.b: nuclear cataract and irregular corneal astigmatism due to epithelial basement membrane dystrophy
options.c: recurrent herpes simplex keratitis with peripheral corneal scarring and moderate nuclear cataract
options.d: nuclear cataract and Fuchs endothelial dystrophy, with vision worse in the morning

pool.rationale: Fluctuating vision that is worse in the morning due to corneal endothelial dysfunction (not tear dysfunction) is an indication for keratoplasty (penetrating or endothelial). Concurrent removal of a cataract is indicated if the cataract is visually significant or likely to pro­gress rapidly. Epithelial basement membrane dystrophy might require corneal debridement, not keratoplasty. Peripheral corneal scarring is unlikely to be visually significant. A dense cataract with mild endothelial dystrophy should generally be treated with cataract surgery alone.

pool.q: Two days ago, an 11-year-old boy was hammering on a taillight of an old car and felt something fly into his right eye. What abnormality is depicted by the white arrows?

options.b: a traumatic cataract with intact anterior capsule
options.c: an anterior capsular tear from 11 o'clock to 4 o'clock
options.d: a large corneal laceration extending from 11 o'clock to 4 o'clock

pool.rationale: The history most likely indicates a metallic foreign body injury. A small foreign body can perforate the cornea and the lens capsule. Trypan blue capsular dye makes visualization of the capsule easier. Trypan blue was used to stain the anterior capsule, and the arrows are pointing to the anterior capsule tear due to the injury. A foreign body, a corneal laceration, or an intact anterior capsule would not show the lack of stain in that region as depicted in the surgical photo.

pool.q: What is the best initial treatment for patients with dysphotopsias from intraocular lenses (IOLs)?

options.c: scheduling the patients for an IOL exchange
options.d: reassuring the patients that dysphotopsias are a common problem that often improves over time

pool.rationale: Positive dysphotopsias, described as glare, streaks, flashes, arcs, or halos, are common with truncated square-edge IOLs and those manufactured from higher-index materials. Negative dysphotopsias are described as an arcuate dark or dim region, usually in the temporal visual field. Most patients who experience dysphotopsias improve with time. Initially, observation is advised. The other options (IOL exchange, pilocarpine 0.5%, and brimonidine 0.2%) can be possible plans if symptoms do not resolve over time, but with caution of the risks involved with each.

pool.q: A 76-year-old man reports chronic progressive decrease in vision of the right eye. He states that he has worn "coke-bottle" glasses since childhood and is borderline diabetic (the condition is currently diet-controlled). What is the most important next step in evaluation and management?

options.d: Refer patient to the retina service.

pool.rationale:
The most important next step after obtaining a history is to assess the best corrected visual acuity in both eyes and determine refractive error. Dilating the patient's eyes is important to do after determining best visual acuity, as is performing gonioscopy if narrow angles are suspected (or any other pathology involving the angle is suspected). The fundus examination after dilation is key for examining the extent of anterior segment pathology such as cataract, and for noting any abnormalities of the retina, such as diabetic retinopathy (possible in this patient with history of diabetes mellitus).
If this patient were determined by refraction to be a high myope, then special attention would be paid to the peripheral retina to rule out lattice degeneration, preexisting retinal holes, vitreoretinal traction, or other conditions that may complicate cataract surgery and/or limit visual potential if surgery were required in this patient. If diabetic retinopathy, particularly neovascularization, macular edema, or retinal ischemia was noted, it may need to be treated prior to cataract surgery to prevent worsening of the retinopathy postoperatively. This would be especially important if posterior capsular rupture occurred during surgery, as the risk of cystoid macular edema, worsening of retinopathy, and/or retinal detachment increases significantly in that circumstance.

pool.q: A patient with recurrent retinal detachments and proliferative vitreoretinopathy undergoes a pars plana vitrectomy with scleral buckling and silicone oil. The patient is subsequently referred to a surgeon for cataract removal. What type of lens implant must be avoided in this patient?
pool.rationale: Nuclear cataract formation is common after pars plana vitrectomy. Posterior subcapsular opacification is typical after use of silicone oil during retinal surgery. Silicone lens implants are contraindicated in these eyes because silicone oil adheres to the implant surface. Acrylic or PMMA IOLs are not contraindicated in eyes that have silicone oil.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Lens & Cataract — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: During a cataract extraction, the red reflex is suddenly lost and there is iris prolapse. What is the next step?

options.d: adjust the lid speculum to decrease posterior pressure

pool.rationale: During ECCE or phacoemulsification, the anterior chamber may become shallow. If the reason for the loss of AC depth or elevated IOP is unknown, the surgeon should check the red reflex to evaluate the possibility of a suprachoroidal hemorrhage or effusion. In these situations, the eye typically becomes very firm, and the patient becomes agitated and reports having pain. Expulsive suprachoroidal hemorrhage presents as a sudden increase in IOP, accompanied by acute onset of pain and darkening of the red reflex, incision gape, iris prolapse and expulsion of the lens, vitreous, and bright red blood. The instant this is recognized, the surgeon must close the incision with sutures or digital pressure. Prolapsed vitreous should be excised and uveal tissue reposited. After the wound is securely closed, the surgeon may consider posterior sclerotomies to allow the escape of suprachoroidal blood to decompress the globe, enable repositioning of prolapsed intraocular tissue, and facilitate permanent closure of the cataract incision.

pool.q: What isolated ocular pathology does the potential acuity meter (PAM) most effectively bypass?
pool.rationale: The potential acuity meter is most helpful in estimating potential visual acuity in patients with a lenticular contribution to vision loss. This test works by projecting a tiny vision chart onto the retina through a small entrance pupil. This test can be misleading in the presence of several disorders, including age-related macular degeneration (AMD), amblyopia, macular edema, glaucoma, macular scars, and serous retinal detachment.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Lens & Cataract — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Toward the completion of nuclear quadrant removal, the cataract surgeon notices a sudden deepening of the anterior chamber and poor aspiration of the remaining nuclear material. What would be the most appropriate next step?

options.a: Inject viscoelastic to maintain the anterior chamber, then inspect the posterior capsule for a break.
options.b: Perform posterior sclerotomies to drain choroidal fluid, then finish the case.
options.c: Increase the aspiration flow rate or vacuum setting to improve aspiration, then continue phacoemulsification.
options.d: Close the wound to prevent loss of intraocular contents, then administer IV mannitol.

pool.rationale:
Sudden deepening of the anterior chamber and diminution of suction effect strongly suggest a breach of posterior capsular integrity. Reducing infusion, injecting viscoelastic to prevent anterior migration of the vitreous, and inspecting for a posterior capsular break are indicated.
Increasing the flow rate would increase the likelihood of increasing a capsular tear and risk irrigating vitreous anteriorly.
Posterior sclerotomies and IV mannitol are indicated for expulsive choroidal hemorrhages, not posterior capsular breaks. In contrast to a posterior capsular breach, an expulsive choroidal hemorrhage presents with a shallowing of the anterior chamber.

pool.q: A 53-year-old patient with ankylosing spondylitis presents for an examination after resolution of his third episode of anterior uveitis. He has been successfully treated with corticosteroid drops. His vision is decreased, with significant glare. What is the most likely cause?
pool.rationale: All of the answer choices are possible sequelae of repeated episodes of anterior uveitis. Posterior subcapsular cataract is routinely associated with glare. Keratic precipitates and synechiae tend not to cause visual symptoms unless very extensive. Cystoid macular edema would cause a decrease in visual acuity, but it would not be associated with glare.

pool.q: What lens changes might be seen after hyperbaric oxygen therapy?
pool.rationale: Hyperbaric oxygen can cause lens changes. Usually it is just a myopic shift, but it can lead to nuclear changes. Posterior subcapsular cataracts are common in diabetes and with prednisone usage. Cortical clefts can occur with extreme glucose shifts.

pool.q: Chronic ultraviolet radiation exposure typically causes what type of cataract?
pool.rationale: Ultraviolet radiation exposure is associated with increased risk of cortical cataracts, perhaps more frequently in men than women. Although sunlight exposure accounts for only approximately 10 percent of the total risk of cortical cataract in the general population in temperate climates, this risk is avoidable. Clinicians should encourage their patients to avoid excessive sunlight exposure. Ultraviolet radiation does not increase the risk of other cataract types.

pool.q: A 65-year-old patient reports increasing glare in both eyes. She was told years ago that she had congenital cataracts. Her examination demonstrates 2+ nuclear sclerosis and round, dense, white, posterior capsular plaques in both eyes. When considering cataract surgery, what special consideration should be anticipated?

options.a: Keeping the anterior chamber highly pressurized will improve safety.
options.b: Aggressive hydrodissection is indicated to remove the plaques.
options.c: There is an increased risk of posterior capsule rupture during phacoemulsification.
options.d: Intraocular lens (IOL) implantation in the capsular bag is contraindicated.

pool.rationale:
The scenario describes a posterior polar cataract.  A weak or absent area of posterior lens capsule in the region of a posterior polar opacity places the eye at increased risk for capsular rupture during cataract surgery. During surgery, the surgeon should avoid creating excessive pressure within the capsular bag. 
Complete hydrodissection is avoided because of possible tearing of the capsule directly under the opacity. After the surgeon places the IOL in the bag (in cases where the capsule is intact), care should be used to minimize capsular bag movement.

pool.q: A 65-year-old, insulin-dependent woman with laser-treated proliferative diabetic retinopathy needs cataract surgery with an IOL implant. Under the operative microscope, the ophthalmologist cannot see a red reflex. What technique is most likely to assure a successful surgical outcome?
pool.rationale: When a patient has a poor or absent red reflex, capsulorrhexis is more difficult, with an increased risk of radial capsular tears. The use of a capsular dye, such as trypan blue, makes anterior capsular visualization clearer, which reduces the likelihood of complication. A poor red reflex may result from a mature cataract or a vitreous opacity such as a vitreous hemorrhage. Based upon the information given, there is no reason to expect this woman to have a vitreous hemorrhage. An iris ring enhances the recognition of a faint red reflex but has no effect in the absence of a red reflex (presence of sufficient media opacity). A silicone IOL is a poor choice in a patient who may need retinal surgery in the future. Indirect ophthalmoscopy would determine if there was a vitreous hemorrhage. An anterior vitrectomy would be insufficient in most diabetic hemorrhages to reconstitute a red reflex.

pool.q: A 45-year-old man presents with a visual acuity of hand motion only in his left eye. The cornea appears clear and there is a dense cataract and a poor view of the posterior segment on indirect ophthalmoscopy. What is the most appropriate test to perform next in evaluating this patient's poor vision?

options.d: optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the retina

pool.rationale: Because there is a poor view of the posterior segment, the surgeon needs to ascertain the status of the vitreous and retina before undertaking cataract surgery. OCT and fluorescein angiography both require a relatively clear media in order to image the retina. Although ERG can be helpful in evaluating indeterminate causes of visual loss, this test is difficult to perform and is not always readily available, and is thus more appropriate when other modalities are inconclusive.

pool.q: A 73-year-old woman had uncomplicated cataract extraction with placement of a 1-piece acrylic posterior chamber intraocular lens (IOL). Initially, her best-corrected vision was 20/20 with a plano correction. Three months later, she returned complaining of gradual blurring of her vision in her eye. Her best corrected vision was 20/20 with a -2.00 diopter lens. What caused the change in her vision?
pool.rationale: Based upon the late postoperative onset of myopic shift, the diagnosis is postoperative capsular contraction. Risk factors include small capsulorrhexis, abnormal or asymmetric zonular support, or use of a silicone plate haptic IOL. A 3-piece lens may be at lower risk for capsular contraction than a 1-piece lens because of increased rigidity of the haptics. Because the initial vision was 20/20 without correction, IOL choice error is unlikely. IOL opacification would not cause a correctable myopic shift. Cystoid macular edema may cause a postoperative change in vision, but would cause a hyperopic shift, not a myopic shift.

pool.q: Three months after cataract surgery, a patient has the fluorescein angiography finding shown. It has not responded to topical medications. What is the best next step in treatment of this condition?
pool.rationale:
The topical medications ketorolac 0.5% and prednisolone acetate 1.0% have been shown to be effective for treating chronic cystoid macular edema (CME). If topical medications fail, sub-Tenon steroid injection or intravitreal injections of corticosteroids alone or via a sustained drug-delivery system may be effective. In refractory cases, systemic carbonic anhydrase inhibitors may be beneficial. Intravitreal vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) inhibitors have been used with success in chronic CME cases that do not respond to conventional treatment.
Surgical therapy may be indicated when an inciting source of chronic CME can be defined and the edema fails to respond to medical therapy. Any retained lens fragments should be removed. Nd:YAG laser vitreolysis or vitrectomy can be used to remove vitreous adhering to the cataract incision in order to relieve iris deformity or vitreomacular traction. If the IOL is malpositioned and contributing to chronic uveitis, repositioning or exchange may be helpful.

pool.q: In what scenario is the use of a 3-piece intraocular lens (IOL) recommended over use of a 1-piece acrylic lens?

options.a: in an eye with a glaucoma drainage implant
options.b: in an eye with a compromised capsular bag and inadequate zonular support
options.c: in an eye with chronic uveitis

pool.rationale: In an eye with compromised capsular bag, a 3-piece lens is recommended for sulcus or scleral fixation. In eyes with chronic uveitis, some surgeons prefer not to use silicone lenses. There is no advantage of IOL type in the case of eyes with history of vitrectomy or glaucoma drainage implant.

pool.q: What type of intraocular lens (IOL) cannot be folded at the time of insertion during cataract surgery?
pool.rationale: PMMA material is not flexible and must be inserted without folding. Silicone, acrylic, and hydrogel materials are flexible and allow insertion through a smaller incision via folding or an injector system.

pool.q: A Mittendorf dot is a remnant of the hyaloid vasculature located where?

options.a: on the posterior pole of the lens

pool.rationale: During embryogenesis, the hyaloid artery supplies nutrients to the developing lens. The hyaloid vasculature usually disappears prior to birth. However, there are cases wherein this regression is not complete. Occasionally, remnants of the hyaloid vasculature can be seen either on the posterior pole of the lens (Mittendorf dot) or on the optic nerve (Bergmeister papilla). There may also be opacities left in the vitreous. Regression of the hyaloid vasculature also leaves a channel through the vitreous (Cloquet canal).

pool.q: One cataract surgeon performs phacoemulsification, making a 2.5-mm scleral tunnel incision superiorly and uses a horizontal mattress stitch to close the sclera. Another cataract surgeon makes a 5-mm clear corneal incision temporally, using a single interrupted stitch to close the corneal wound. Why is one of these incisions more likely than the other to result in a surgically induced postoperative astigmatism?

options.a: The scleral tunnel incision is more likely to cause astigmatism; that is a risk of performing a scleral tunnel incision.
options.b: The scleral tunnel incision is more likely to cause astigmatism because of the horizontal mattress stitch.
options.c: The corneal incision is more likely to cause astigmatism because of the temporal location.
options.d: The corneal incision is more likely to cause astigmatism because of the wound length.

pool.rationale:
A corneal, scleral, or limbal incision of less than 3 mm in length will generally induce less than 1 diopter (Δ) of astigmatism. Incisions that require suture closure are likely to induce additional astigmatism. In this scenario, the first surgeon has 1 factor that could increase postoperative astigmatism, while the second surgeon has 2 factors that could increase postoperative astigmatism.
A small incision is unlikely to induce much, if any corneal astigmatism. If a larger corneal incision is required, placing it across the steeper meridian may reduce astigmatism. One advantage of the scleral tunnel incision is that it creates an internal cornea lip that may reduce the incidence of both early and late surgically induced astigmatism.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Lens & Cataract — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What usually causes uveitis-glaucoma-hyphema (UGH) syndrome?
pool.rationale: Uveitis-glaucoma-hyphema (UGH) syndrome was first described in the context of rigid or closed-loop anterior chamber intraocular lenses (ACIOLs). Decentration of a posterior chamber IOL (PCIOL) can also lead to UGH syndrome due to contact with uveal tissue. UGH syndrome can result from inappropriate IOL sizing, contact between the implant and vascular structures or the corneal endothelium, or a defect in the implant manufacturing. Crystalline lenses and aphakia do not cause this problem.

pool.q: An ophthalmologist is performing a routine phacoemulsification when she notes that the remaining half of the nucleus has suddenly dropped through an open posterior capsule and appears to be suspended on the anterior vitreous face. What is the best next step?

options.a: lollipopping the nucleus with the phaco tip in order to pull it into the anterior chamber
options.b: immediate withdrawal of the phaco instrument and any secondary instrument from the eye
options.c: injection of viscoelastic to stabilize the anterior chamber
options.d: vigorous irrigation with a balanced salt solution (BSS) to swill the remaining nucleus into the anterior chamber

pool.rationale:
If capsule rupture occurs during phacoemulsification, lens fragments may enter the posterior segment. At the time of posterior capsule rupture, the surgeon should stabilize the anterior chamber by reducing the high fluid flow and vacuum levels, and by compartmentalizing the vitreous with ophthalmic viscosurgical device (OVD) before removing the phaco instrument.
Surgeons should avoid immediate withdrawal of the phaco instrument from the eye, because that would result in an outward pressure gradient, bringing more vitreous forward into the anterior chamber and outward toward the incisions. OVD can also be introduced posterior to a suspended nuclear fragment in an effort to float it anteriorly.
Insertion of a second instrument or lens glide behind the nuclear remnant may help prevent the remnant from being dislocated into the vitreous, whereas attempts to impale the nuclear fragment with the phaco tip may force the fragment posteriorly by either the tip or the irrigation, as might also happen if attempting to swill the fragment with vigorous BSS irrigation.
Lollipopping the nuclear fragment with the phaco tip may force it back and may transect the fragment, exposing the aspiration port and increasing the risk of aspirating vitreous.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Lens & Cataract — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What postoperative complication may result from the creation of a 3.5 mm capsulorrhexis during cataract surgery?
pool.rationale: Capsular phimosis syndrome occurs when the anterior capsule contracts, resulting in decentration of an IOL optic. Smaller capsulorrhexis (such as 3.5 mm in this question), pseudoexfoliation syndrome, or focal zonular weakness predispose to this condition. IOL glistenings are reduced with a larger capsulorrhexis with piggybacking lenses; however, there is no mention of piggybacking in this question. Sunrise syndrome occurs when the superior haptic is in the sulcus, allowing the IOL to dislocate superiorly. Pupillary capture can occur when the IOL is displaced anteriorly, which would be more common with a large capsulorrhexis.

pool.q: What is a common risk factor for suprachoroidal hemorrhage associated with cataract surgery?
pool.rationale:
Suprachoroidal effusion and suprachoroidal hemorrhage have been associated with
  • hypertension
  • arteriosclerotic cardiovascular disease
  • tachycardia
  • obesity
  • high myopia
  • glaucoma
  • advanced age
  • nanophthalmos
  • choroidal hemangioma associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome
  • chronic ocular inflammation

pool.q: What complication is of particular concern during cataract surgery on an intumescent cataract?
pool.rationale:
An intumescent cataract is swollen and enlarged with cortical material that often envelops a hard nucleus floating within the capsular bag. This type of cataract presents specific challenges during phacoemulsification cataract surgery. Intumescent cataracts have weak zonular fibers and fragile capsules. Because intumescence creates positive pressure in the capsular bag, the initial incision in the capsule may extend peripherally.
Phacolytic glaucoma, not angle-closure glaucoma, can occur due to leakage of lens protein through the capsule of a mature or hypermature cataract. There is no increased risk of corneal edema or choroidal effusion.

pool.q: A 72-year-old woman has function-limiting visual blurring OD. Her visual acuity OD is 20/200 wearing -1.75 sphere. Manifest refraction improves her visual acuity to 20/50 with a correction of -4.00 sph. Given her findings shown, what management is recommended?
pool.rationale: The figure shows a moderately brunescent nuclear sclerotic cataract. Given her refraction, the preferred next step would be to consent the patient for cataract surgery. LASIK is not appropriate in this situation, for it would not provide vision correction. While diabetes is associated with this type of cataract, addressing this area would not address her visual needs or rehabilitation. In cases with milder cataract, the clinician can ask how the patient is currently doing with activities of daily living and can discuss how much improvement a new spectacle prescription or contact lens use could provide. In this case of more significant cataract, neither contact lenses nor glasses will provide enough visual improvement; thus, cataract surgery is the better choice. Except in the case of a medical need to remove a cataract (eg, phacomorphic or phacolytic glaucoma), it is usually preferable to listen to the patient's needs and consider how the patient’s vision is affecting his or her lifestyle.

pool.q: What change occurs in the lens and zonule when the ciliary muscle contracts?

options.b: The dioptric power of the lens decreases.
options.c: The equatorial diameter of the lens decreases.
options.d: The axial length of the lens decreases.

pool.rationale: When the ciliary muscle contracts, the diameter of the muscle ring is reduced. As a result, the zonular tension decreases and the axial thickness of the lens increases, the equatorial diameter of the lens decreases, and the dioptric power of the lens increases.

pool.q: The majority of high-energy phosphate bonds required for lens metabolism are provided by what pathway?
pool.rationale: The goal of lens metabolism is the maintenance of lens transparency. In the lens, energy production largely depends on glucose metabolism. Glucose enters the lens from the aqueous humor both by simple diffusion and by a mediated transfer process called facilitated diffusion. Most of the glucose transported into the lens is phosphorylated to glucose-6-phosphate (G6P) by the enzyme hexokinase. Once formed, G6P enters 1 of 2 metabolic pathways: anaerobic glycolysis or the hexose monophosphate (HMP) shunt. The more active of these 2 pathways is anaerobic glycolysis, which provides most of the high-energy phosphate bonds required for lens metabolism. This pathway is much less efficient than aerobic glycolysis, because only 2 net molecules of ATP are produced for each glucose molecule utilized, whereas aerobic glycolysis produces an additional 36 molecules of ATP from each glucose molecule metabolized in the citric acid cycle (oxidative metabolism). Because of the low oxygen tension in the lens, only about 3% of the lens glucose passes through the citric acid cycle (also called the tricarboxylic acid cycle or the Krebs cycle) to produce ATP; however, even this low level of aerobic metabolism produces approximately 25% of the lens ATP.

pool.q: Following tennis ball trauma, a 32-year-old man develops a cataract. At the slit lamp, he has mild iridodonesis, but no lens subluxation or dislocation is appreciated. What finding would indicate that a pars plana approach would be preferred to an anterior approach?

options.a: anterior capsular rupture with cortical material in the anterior chamber
options.c: two clock hours of zonular dehiscence
options.d: poor visibility of lens when patient is supine

pool.rationale:
Iridodonesis detected at the slit lamp may be the initial finding that signals zonular weakness or absence. In some cases, the zonular fibers that remain may tether the lens within the anterior vitreous such that when the patient sits upright at the slit lamp, the lens seems accessible for extraction. However, when the patient is supine during surgery, the lens may tilt backward and out of the surgeon's reach. Thus, when iridodonesis or phacodonesis is detected preoperatively, it is helpful to confirm lens position with the patient supine during the preoperative examination.
Nasal iridodialysis and anterior capsular rupture are not contraindications to an anterior approach. If zonular dehiscence over 120 degrees is present, intracapsular or extracapsular cataract extraction may be considered.

pool.q: What operative factor contributes to microscope-induced light toxicity during ocular surgery?

options.b: microscope filters with a 500-nm wavelength cutoff

pool.rationale: Longer operating times contribute to photic injury. Microscope filters and tilting the microscope reduce the risk of photic injury. It has not been shown or claimed that the use of viscoelastic significantly reduces photic injury. Prolonged exposure to the illuminating filament of the operating microscope can result in an increased risk of cystoid macular edema or a burn to the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). The risk of an RPE burn is particularly high during cataract surgery, when the light-absorbing effects of the natural lens (cataract) are removed. This maneuver exposes the RPE to minimally attenuated blue and near-ultraviolet radiation. If the photic injury occurs in or adjacent to the fovea, visual acuity may be reduced. If the injury is extrafoveal, the patient may develop a paracentral scotoma. Minimizing retinal exposure to the operating microscope light, and keeping operating times as short as possible, help reduce this complication. Other actions to reduce the risk of retinal photic injury include using the minimum light intensity needed to safely perform the procedure, always using manufacturer-approved lamps, using a filter to attenuate wavelengths below 515 nm, using oblique lighting when possible, using pupillary shields, and minimizing direct exposure of the fovea.

pool.q: Cataract surgery in a patient with keratoconjunctivitis sicca secondary to collagen vascular disease may have an increased risk of what postoperative complications?
pool.rationale: Patients with keratoconjunctivitis sicca associated with collagen vascular disease, pemphigoid, rheumatoid arthritis, or Sjögren syndrome present a special challenge to the cataract surgeon. Postoperatively, there is a risk of toxic keratoconjunctivitis and corneal ulceration, particularly with the use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and corneal ulceration. There is not an increased risk of endophthalmitis, macular edema, or uveitis.

pool.q: What lens abnormality is portrayed here?
pool.rationale: This patient has an anterior polar cataract. Anterior polar cataracts are an opacity of the anterior subcapsular cortex and capsule. They are frequently autosomal dominant and often visually asymptomatic. In most cases, they are nonprogressive. A Mittendorf dot, a common anomalous variant noted in many healthy eyes, is a small, dense, white spot on the posterior surface of the posterior lens capsule typically located inferonasal to the visual axis. The slit-lamp view localizes this lesion to the anterior pole of the lens, which eliminates a posterior polar or posterior subcapsular cataract.

pool.q: What complication risk is increased in patients using chlorpromazine when undergoing cataract extraction?
pool.rationale:
Intraoperative floppy iris syndrome (IFIS) refers to the intraoperative triad of billowing or floppiness of the iris, prolapse of the iris into incisions, and progressive pupillary miosis. IFIS can result in higher rates of complications such as iris trauma, posterior capsular rupture, and vitreous loss. Tamsulosin, a selective alpha-1a adrenergic antagonist, has been associated with IFIS, but now nonselective alpha adrenergic antagonists and antipsychotics with alpha adrenergic activity such as chlorpromazine have also been reported to cause IFIS.
Descemet membrane detachment occurs when an instrument is inadvertently placed into or fluid is injected between Descemet membrane and the corneal stroma. Aqueous misdirection occurs due to ciliolenticular block with anterior movement of the iris-lens interface, shallowing of the anterior chamber, choroidal expansion, and poor conductivity of fluid through the vitreous leading to elevated intraocular pressure. It is more common in eyes with prior angle closure following intraocular surgery.

pool.q: What procedure is best suited for cataract extraction in an eye with controlled uveitis?

options.a: phacoemulsification without placement of an intraocular lens
options.b: phacoemulsification and placement of an acrylic intraocular lens (IOL) in the capsular bag
options.c: extracapsular cataract extraction and placement of a one-piece acrylic lens in the sulcus
options.d: phacoemulsification and placement of a silicone IOL in the capsular bag

pool.rationale: Acrylic IOLs are generally well tolerated and preferred over a silicone IOL because of the risk of inflammatory precipitates collecting on the silicone IOL surface postoperatively. When complications arise and a lens cannot be inserted into the capsular bag, it may be advisable to omit placing a lens in the ciliary sulcus or implanting an anterior chamber lens. Other options may include leaving the patient aphakic or using a scleral-fixated lens. One-piece acrylic lenses should never be placed in the ciliary sulcus, because they can lead to iris chafing and inflammation.
